domains.name: JVM Internals
domains.description: Class loading, bytecode, JIT compilation, garbage collection, and the memory model — how Java actually runs.

scenarios.title: The ClassNotFoundException that compiled fine
scenarios.situation: Your service starts in staging but throws ClassNotFoundException for a class that compiled fine. The same fat JAR works locally. The class lives in a dependency your module declares.
objectives: Diagnose runtime classpath vs compile classpath mismatches
evidence: Compile scope includes a dependency (e.g. provided scope) that is absent at runtime, so javac sees it but the app loader does not.
Two JARs export the same package; the module system refuses and the unnamed module picks one arbitrarily.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and what is the correct fix?
choices: A. The JVM's bootstrap loader does not load application classes; add the JAR to the boot classpath.
B. A split-package or visibility issue across module/class-loader boundaries; inspect the runtime classpath and module graph with -XshowSettings or jdeps, then fix the dependency scope.
C. The JIT compiler eliminated the class; disable tiered compilation with -XX:-TieredCompilation.
D. The class file version is too new; the fix is always to recompile everything with an older javac.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the compiler and the JVM at runtime do not see the same classpath.
scenarios.why: The JVM loads classes through a delegation hierarchy: bootstrap (JDK), platform, then application class loaders, and each loader only sees what its parent and its own classpath expose. ClassNotFoundException at runtime with a clean compile almost always means the runtime classpath differs from the compile classpath — a dependency with provided/test scope, a split package across modules, or a container that isolates class loaders. Tools like jdeps and -XshowSettings:properties reveal the real runtime view; the boot classpath and JIT are red herrings here.

scenarios.title: The interviewer asks what invokedynamic does
scenarios.situation: In a senior Java interview you are asked: 'javac emits bytecode — what does invokedynamic do, and why does it matter for lambdas?' You know lambdas are not anonymous inner classes anymore.
objectives: Explain invokedynamic and the LambdaMetafactory bootstrap
Read javap -c output for lambda call sites
evidence: Observed: In a senior Java interview you are asked: 'javac emits bytecode — what does invokedynamic do, and why does it matter for lambdas?' You know lambdas are not anonymous inner classes anymore. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain invokedynamic and the LambdaMetafactory bootstrap (2) Read javap -c output for lambda call sites Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: Which answer demonstrates real understanding?
choices: A. invokedynamic calls a method dynamically using reflection, which is why lambdas are slower than anonymous classes.

B. invokedynamic delegates the call-site linkage to a bootstrap method at first execution; lambdas use it so the JVM can generate the implementation class at runtime (via LambdaMetafactory) instead of javac emitting an anonymous class per lambda.
C. invokedynamic is how the JIT inlines virtual methods; it has nothing to do with lambdas.
D. invokedynamic replaces the constant pool; lambdas store their bodies directly in the constant pool.
scenarios.hint: Hint: think about who decides HOW the lambda object gets created — javac, or the runtime?
scenarios.why: invokedynamic (JSR 292) was added so the JVM could support dynamically-typed languages, but its killer app in Java 8+ is lambdas. When javac compiles a lambda it emits an invokedynamic instruction pointing at the LambdaMetafactory bootstrap method. The first time the instruction executes, the bootstrap method runs and links the call site to a runtime-generated class implementing the functional interface. This defers the strategy decision to runtime: the JDK can change how lambdas are materialized without recompiling your code, and it avoids one class file per lambda. It is not reflection (choice A) and not a JIT inlining mechanism (choice C) — it is late binding of the call site itself.

scenarios.title: The benchmark that proved nothing
scenarios.situation: A teammate benchmarks two JSON parsers with a hand-rolled loop: parse once, time it, declare a winner. You suspect the numbers are meaningless because the JVM was still warming up.
evidence: Observed: A teammate benchmarks two JSON parsers with a hand-rolled loop: parse once, time it, declare a winner. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain tiered compilation and warmup (2) Design a valid JMH microbenchmark Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the technically correct explanation of what is wrong, and the right fix?
choices: A. The garbage collector pauses during the first parse; run with -Xmx1g to fix the benchmark.

B. The first iterations run in the interpreter (or C1) while profiling data is gathered; only after a method is hot does C2 compile optimized machine code. A single untimed warmup makes the measurement reflect unoptimized code. Use JMH with warmup iterations.
C. The JIT only optimizes static methods; instance-method benchmarks are always invalid.
D. Class loading dominates; the fix is to run the benchmark in a static initializer.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what is the JVM doing during the first few thousand iterations that it is not doing later?
scenarios.why: The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode while the profilers in C1 (client) tier collect branch and type statistics. Once a method crosses the hotness threshold, C2 (server) compiles it with speculative optimizations — inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling — guarded by assumptions from the profile. Timing cold code measures the interpreter plus compilation overhead, not steady-state performance, and the JIT can even eliminate dead code (a benchmark whose result is unused may compile to nothing). JMH exists precisely to defeat these traps: warmup iterations, blackholes that prevent dead-code elimination, and forked JVMs. Tiered compilation (C1 then C2) is the default on modern JVMs, not 'static methods only' or GC pauses.

scenarios.title: The 200-millisecond pause at peak traffic
scenarios.situation: Your low-latency trading service sees 200 ms stop-the-world pauses at peak, correlated with old-gen collections. Heap is 16 GB, allocation rate is high, and the SLA demands p99 under 20 ms.
objectives: Match GC choice to latency vs throughput requirements
Read GC logs to verify pause behavior
evidence: Observed: Your low-latency trading service sees 200 ms stop-the-world pauses at peak, correlated with old-gen collections. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Match GC choice to latency vs throughput requirements (2) Read GC logs to verify pause behavior Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: Which GC strategy best fits, and why?
choices: A. Keep Parallel GC and double the heap to 32 GB — larger heaps always mean shorter pauses.
B. Switch to ZGC (or Shenandoah): a low-pause collector that does most work concurrently, trading some throughput for sub-10 ms pauses even on large heaps.
C. Switch to Serial GC: a single-threaded collector has the least coordination overhead, so pauses shrink.
D. Disable GC with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC and rely on Epsilon GC in production for zero pauses.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the SLA is about pause time, and pauses scale with the collector's stop-the-world phases.
scenarios.why: Pause time, not heap size, is the binding constraint: Parallel GC's stop-the-world full collections scale with live-set size, so a bigger heap often makes pauses worse, not better (choice A is backwards). ZGC and Shenandoah are concurrent collectors — marking, relocation, and reference processing happen alongside application threads, with only brief stop-the-world phases (root scanning, typically sub-millisecond to a few ms). They sacrifice some throughput (concurrent work competes with the app; ZGC historically caps around ~15% overhead) to hold pauses flat as the heap grows, which is exactly the p99-latency trade this service needs. Serial GC minimizes total CPU but maximizes pause time (choice C is inverted), and Epsilon never collects — it is a testing tool that will OOM the service (choice D is a production outage).

scenarios.title: The container that OOMs with heap to spare
scenarios.situation: Your service runs in a container with a 2 GB limit. -Xmx is 1 GB, heap metrics look healthy, but the container keeps getting OOM-killed. Native memory tracking shows Metaspace and thread stacks growing without bound.
objectives: Account for all JVM memory consumers beyond the heap
Use NMT to diagnose container OOM kills
evidence: Observed: Your service runs in a container with a 2 GB limit. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Account for all JVM memory consumers beyond the heap (2) Use NMT to diagnose container OOM kills Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and what is the correct response?
choices: A. The heap is fine so this is a kernel bug; raise the container limit and move on.

B. Memory outside the heap — Metaspace (class metadata), thread stacks, direct ByteBuffers, and JIT code cache — is consuming the container limit. Cap Metaspace, reduce thread count (or move to virtual threads), and track native memory with NMT.
C. -Xmx only limits young gen; set -Xmn to cap the rest of native memory.
D. The JVM ignores container limits on Java 17; the only fix is upgrading to Java 21.
scenarios.hint: Hint: -Xmx is not the process's memory limit — what else does a JVM allocate?
scenarios.why: -Xmx caps only the Java heap. A JVM process also holds Metaspace (class metadata, unbounded by default), one stack per platform thread (default 1 MB each — a thousand threads is a gigabyte), direct ByteBuffers allocated outside the heap, the JIT code cache, and GC bookkeeping. In a container, the cgroup limit applies to the whole process, so healthy heap metrics with OOM kills means the leak is off-heap. The JVM has respected container limits since Java 10 (choice D is outdated), and -Xmx/ -Xmn only subdivide the heap (choice C is wrong about what they control). The fix is measuring with Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=detail, jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory) and capping the actual consumers: -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, fewer platform threads, bounded direct-buffer caches.

scenarios.title: The profiler that lied about the hotspot
scenarios.situation: A sampling profiler says 40% of CPU is in a logging method, so the team rewrites the logger. Production is unchanged. A second look with Java Flight Recorder and async-profiler shows the real hotspot is lock contention in a cache.
objectives: Choose wall-clock profiling + contention events for latency work
evidence: Observed: A sampling profiler says 40% of CPU is in a logging method, so the team rewrites the logger. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain safepoint bias (2) Choose wall-clock profiling + contention events for latency work Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: Why did the first profiler mislead, and what is the reliable approach?
choices: A. Sampling profilers are always wrong; only instrumentation profilers give true data.

B. The first profiler suffered safepoint bias — it could only sample at safepoints, over-representing code that runs at safepoints and hiding blocked/waiting time. JFR and async-profiler sample independently of safepoints (and capture lock/wait events), revealing contention.
C. The logger really was the hotspot but the rewrite introduced a new bottleneck that exactly canceled the gain.
D. Profilers cannot measure lock contention at all; the second result was also wrong.
scenarios.hint: Hint: a CPU sampler shows where threads are running. Where are the threads that are NOT running?
scenarios.why: Classic JVM profilers that rely on GetCallTrace at safepoints systematically over-sample methods that happen to execute at safepoints (like allocation-heavy or call-heavy code) and under-sample everything else — this is safepoint bias. Worse, CPU-time profilers show where threads RUN, not where they WAIT: lock contention appears as idle time, invisible to a pure CPU sampler, so the team optimized the wrong thing. JFR records JVM-level events (including jdk.JavaMonitorEnter for blocked threads and allocation events) with negligible overhead and can run in production; async-profiler samples with perf_events independently of safepoints and can attribute wall-clock time including lock waits. The reliable approach is wall-clock profiling plus contention events, not 'instrumentation only' (choice A overcorrects — instrumentation distorts inlining and adds heavy overhead).

domains.name: Spring Boot
domains.description: Autoconfiguration, dependency injection, REST APIs, data access, and production observability with Spring Boot.

scenarios.title: The bean that appeared from nowhere
scenarios.situation: Your Spring Boot app connects to a database you never configured explicitly. A teammate asks where the DataSource bean comes from, and what would happen if you added your own.
evidence: Observed: Your Spring Boot app connects to a database you never configured explicitly. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain conditional autoconfiguration (2) Override an auto-configured bean deliberately Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: Which explanation is correct?
choices: A. Spring Boot scans the classpath; when it finds the JDBC driver and spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, DataSourceAutoConfiguration creates a DataSource bean. A user-defined DataSource bean backs it off via @ConditionalOnMissingBean.
B. Spring Boot always creates a DataSource pointing at localhost; you must override it in every app.
C. Autoconfiguration only works with an application.properties file present; without it no beans are created.
D. The DataSource is created by the servlet container, not Spring; Boot just documents it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what does Spring Boot look at to decide which auto-configurations apply?
scenarios.why: Autoconfiguration is conditional bean registration driven by the classpath: spring.factories / AutoConfiguration.imports lists candidate configurations, each guarded by @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, and friends. Finding HikariCP + the JPA starter on the classpath triggers DataSourceAutoConfiguration, which builds a pooled DataSource from spring.datasource.* properties. Because the auto bean is conditional on missing user beans, defining your own DataSource (or excluding the auto-config) cleanly overrides the default — no XML, no manual wiring. This is why 'it just works' locally and also why a stray starter JAR on the classpath can silently change behavior: conditions, not magic.

scenarios.title: The NullPointerException in the unit test
scenarios.situation: A service uses field injection (@Autowired on a private field). It works in production but throws NullPointerException in a plain unit test. The team debates the right fix.
objectives: Explain bean scopes and proxy pitfalls
evidence: Observed: A service uses field injection (@Autowired on a private field). Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply constructor injection (2) Explain bean scopes and proxy pitfalls Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct engineering answer?
choices: A. Keep field injection and use reflection (ReflectionTestUtils) in tests to set the field — production behavior is what matters.
B. Switch to constructor injection: dependencies become explicit, final, and required; the class is instantiable with plain 'new' in tests without any Spring context.
C. Make the field static so tests can set it once for all test methods.
D. Annotate the test with @SpringBootTest so the full context wires the field — unit tests should always boot the container.
scenarios.hint: Hint: which style lets you write new OrderService(fakeRepo) in a test with no framework?
scenarios.why: Field injection hides required dependencies: the class cannot be constructed in a valid state without the container, so plain unit tests need reflection hacks or a booted context. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit parameters — the compiler enforces they are provided, they can be final (immutable wiring), and a test does new OrderService(mockRepo) with Mockito stubs and no Spring at all. This is why the Spring team itself recommends constructor injection: it turns wiring errors into compile errors and keeps unit tests fast and container-free. Static mutable state (choice C) shares fixtures across tests and creates order-dependent failures; booting the full context for a unit test (choice D) turns milliseconds into seconds per test.

scenarios.title: The 200 OK that meant failure
scenarios.situation: Your API returns 200 OK with {"status": "error"} in the body when an order is not found. Mobile clients cannot distinguish success from failure without parsing bodies, and caching proxies cache the error.
evidence: Observed: Your API returns 200 OK with {"status": "error"} in the body when an order is not found. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design status-code-correct REST endpoints (2) Centralize error handling with @ControllerAdvice Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct REST design?
choices: A. Keep 200 for everything and document the status field — clients already parse JSON anyway.

B. Return proper HTTP status codes (404 for missing, 400 for bad input, 422/409 for conflicts) with a consistent error body (e.g. RFC 7807 problem details); use @ControllerAdvice to translate exceptions centrally.
C. Return 500 for all errors — it is the only status every client understands.
D. Encode the real status in a custom X-Status header and keep 200.
scenarios.hint: Hint: who else reads your status codes besides your own client code?
scenarios.why: HTTP status codes are the API's first-class error channel: intermediaries (caches, load balancers, client libraries) all act on them, and a 200-with-error-body actively misleads them — a caching proxy will happily cache your 'error' as a successful response. The correct pattern is semantic statuses plus a machine-readable error body: Spring's @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods (or ResponseEntityExceptionHandler) maps domain exceptions to statuses once, centrally, so controllers stay clean. RFC 7807 problem-details bodies (type/title/status/detail) give clients a stable contract to parse. Bean Validation (@Valid + @NotNull etc.) on request DTOs turns bad input into 400s before your code runs — validation belongs at the boundary, not scattered through services.

scenarios.title: The endpoint that fires 10,001 queries
scenarios.situation: An endpoint listing 10,000 orders with their line items fires 10,001 SQL queries and times out. The repository is a standard JpaRepository with a derived findAll().
objectives: Choose between entity graphs, fetch joins, and projections
evidence: Observed: An endpoint listing 10,000 orders with their line items fires 10,001 SQL queries and times out. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Diagnose and fix N+1 queries (2) Choose between entity graphs, fetch joins, and projections Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and what is the correct fix?
choices: A. The database is slow; add an index on the orders table primary key.

B. Lazy loading: each order's line-items collection triggers one extra query when accessed (N+1). Fix with a fetch join (@EntityGraph or JOIN FETCH) or a DTO projection so the data loads in one query.
C. JPA always fires N+1 queries; the only fix is rewriting the endpoint in raw JDBC.
D. Increase the HikariCP pool size so the 10,001 queries run in parallel.
scenarios.hint: Hint: count the queries — one for the list, then one per row. What triggers the per-row queries?
scenarios.why: This is the classic N+1: findAll() loads N orders in one query, then accessing each order's lazily-loaded lineItems collection fires one query per order. Lazy loading is correct as a default (you rarely want the whole object graph), but serializing an entity graph to JSON walks every lazy association. The fix keeps JPA: a fetch join (JOIN FETCH o.lineItems or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lineItems")) loads orders plus items in one query, or a DTO projection (interface/class-based) selects exactly the columns the response needs. More connections (choice D) just parallelize the pathology; the primary key is already indexed (choice A misses the point); and abandoning JPA (choice C) throws away the fix that is one annotation away.

scenarios.situation: The service was down for 20 minutes before anyone noticed: the load balancer health check hit / and got 200 from the web layer while the database pool was exhausted. No metrics, no alerts.
objectives: Expose and alert on saturation metrics
evidence: Observed: The service was down for 20 minutes before anyone noticed: the load balancer health check hit / and got 200 from the web layer while the database pool was exhausted. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Configure liveness/readiness probes (2) Expose and alert on saturation metrics Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What should the production setup have included?
choices: A. Nothing — health checks on / are standard; the database recovered on its own eventually.

B. Spring Boot Actuator with a real readiness/liveness split (/actuator/health with db and disk contributors), Micrometer metrics (pool usage, latency histograms) exported to a monitoring system, and alerts on saturation signals.
C. A cron job that restarts the service every hour to clear pool exhaustion.
D. More log lines — if DEBUG had been on, someone would have seen it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the health check answered 'the web server is up' when the question was 'can this instance serve traffic?'
scenarios.why: A health check that only proves the web layer is up is worse than useless — it tells the load balancer to keep sending traffic to a dead service. Actuator's /actuator/health aggregates HealthIndicators (DataSourceHealthIndicator pings the pool, DiskSpaceHealthIndicator checks disk) and Kubernetes distinguishes liveness (restart me) from readiness (stop sending traffic). Micrometer exposes the saturation signals that predict outages: hikaricp_connections_active vs max, http_server_requests_seconds histograms for latency, jvm_memory_used. Alerts fire on those (pool saturation > 80% for 5 min), not on the outage itself. Hourly restarts (choice C) treat the symptom and guarantee data loss windows; DEBUG logs (choice D) are not a monitoring strategy.

scenarios.title: The service that won't start after a merge
scenarios.situation: After a routine merge, the Spring Boot service fails at startup with a BeanCreationException deep in a stack trace. The team is reverting commits at random. You have five minutes before the deploy window closes.
evidence: Observed: After a routine merge, the Spring Boot service fails at startup with a BeanCreationException deep in a stack trace. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Triage Spring startup failures Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined triage order?
choices: A. Read the stack trace bottom-up: find the root cause (the 'Caused by' chain), check the condition evaluation report for conflicting beans, then bisect the merge — random reverts waste the window.
B. Immediately revert the entire merge — startup failures are always caused by the latest commit.
C. Delete the local Maven repository and rebuild; corrupted jars cause most BeanCreationExceptions.
D. Increase startup timeout; bean creation just needs more time after a merge.
scenarios.hint: Hint: Spring prints the answer — but it prints it at the bottom of the stack trace.
scenarios.why: Spring startup failures print a 'Caused by' chain — the LAST caused-by is usually the real error (a missing property, a circular reference, an unsatisfied dependency), while the top frames are just the container unwinding. Reading bottom-up takes seconds and names the culprit; the condition evaluation report (--debug) then shows which auto-configs and user beans collided. Only then, if the cause is not obvious, bisect the merge — random reverts (choice B) burn the deploy window and teach nothing. Corrupted jars (choice C) produce very different errors (ZipException, ClassNotFound), and bean creation does not need 'more time' (choice D) — it failed, deterministically.

domains.name: Testing with JUnit
domains.description: JUnit 5, Mockito, parameterized and integration tests, Testcontainers, and mutation testing — a testing strategy that catches real bugs.

scenarios.title: The test suite that tests one thing 40 times
scenarios.situation: A test class has 40 nearly identical @Test methods, each testing one input value for a tax calculator. Adding a new bracket means copy-pasting another method, and one copy has a typo that has been failing silently.
evidence: Observed: A test class has 40 nearly identical @Test methods, each testing one input value for a tax calculator. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Write parameterized tests (2) Use JUnit 5 lifecycle correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct JUnit 5 approach?
choices: A. Keep the 40 methods; explicit tests are clearer than clever frameworks.
B. Replace them with one @ParameterizedTest fed by @MethodSource or @CsvSource: each input becomes a named case, adding a bracket means adding a row, and @DisplayName documents intent.
C. Delete 39 of the tests; one representative input is enough for a pure function.
D. Move the 40 cases into a spreadsheet and test manually each release.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the bug is in the duplication, not in any single test.
scenarios.why: @ParameterizedTest with @MethodSource/@CsvSource/@EnumSource turns 40 copy-pasted methods into one test method plus a data table — the test logic is written once, each row runs as an independently reported case, and a typo in one row fails loudly instead of hiding in a duplicated method. JUnit 5's @DisplayName and named arguments make the report readable ('bracket [50000, 75000] => 12500'), and the lifecycle (@BeforeEach for fresh fixtures) keeps cases isolated. One representative input (choice C) abandons boundary coverage where tax bugs live; manual spreadsheets (choice D) are not regression tests at all.

scenarios.title: The test that mocks the class under test
scenarios.situation: A test mocks the service it is testing, stubs every method, and asserts the stubs return what was stubbed. It passes always and tests nothing. The team calls it 'unit testing'.
evidence: Observed: A test mocks the service it is testing, stubs every method, and asserts the stubs return what was stubbed. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply mocking discipline (2) Distinguish stubs from interaction verification Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct mocking discipline?
choices: A. It is fine — mocking everything isolates the test from all dependencies including itself.

B. Never mock the class under test; mock its collaborators (dependencies) at architectural boundaries, stub their responses, invoke the REAL object, and verify outcomes — mocks are for dependencies you do not own or that are slow/side-effecting.
C. Never use mocks at all; only integration tests have value.
D. Mock everything except the class under test, including value objects and JDK classes like List.
scenarios.hint: Hint: if the test would pass with an empty implementation of the class, what is it actually testing?
scenarios.why: A mock of the class under test asserts against the test's own stubs — it verifies the mocking framework, not the code. Mocks exist to replace dependencies that are slow, non-deterministic, or outside your control (databases, HTTP clients, clocks): you stub the collaborator, exercise the real unit, and assert on the unit's observable behavior (return values, state changes, and — sparingly — interactions via verify). Value objects and JDK collections (choice D's List) are cheap and deterministic — mocking them adds brittleness for zero isolation benefit. 'No mocks at all' (choice C) throws away the fastest feedback loop you have; the discipline is mocking at boundaries, not mocking nothing.

scenarios.title: The integration test that passes and lies
scenarios.situation: Integration tests run against H2, but production runs Postgres. A query using a Postgres-specific function passes in CI and explodes on deploy. The team debates fixing the query or fixing the tests.
objectives: Run integration tests against real containers
evidence: Observed: Integration tests run against H2, but production runs Postgres. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Run integration tests against real containers (2) Wire container properties dynamically Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct strategy?
choices: A. Fix the query to be H2-compatible — the test database defines the supported SQL dialect.

B. Test against the real dependency: Testcontainers spins up a Dockerized Postgres per test run, so the SQL dialect, types, and constraints under test are the production ones. H2 compatibility is the wrong target.
C. Skip database tests in CI; test SQL manually before releases.
D. Replace Postgres with H2 in production for consistency.
scenarios.hint: Hint: which database's quirks do you want your tests to enforce — the fake one's or production's?
scenarios.why: H2 (or HSQLDB) in 'Postgres compatibility mode' is a different database wearing a costume: dialects, type coercion, constraint behavior, and function libraries all differ, so green tests prove nothing about production SQL. Testcontainers starts a real Postgres container (via JUnit 5 @Testcontainers + @Container, or Spring Boot's @ServiceConnection) and your tests run against the actual engine — the failing function fails in CI, where it belongs. Container startup cost is real but manageable (Ryuk-less reusable containers, singleton container patterns), and it is dwarfed by the cost of a production SQL explosion. Dumbing the query down to H2's dialect (choice A) lets the test double dictate production design — backwards.

scenarios.title: The 95% coverage suite that missed the bug
scenarios.situation: Coverage is 95%, but a one-character production bug (a < that should be <=) shipped. Every line was 'covered'. The team asks what coverage is actually worth.
objectives: Run PIT and triage surviving mutants
evidence: Observed: Coverage is 95%, but a one-character production bug (a < that should be <=) shipped. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain mutation testing vs coverage (2) Run PIT and triage surviving mutants Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does mutation testing add that line coverage cannot?
choices: A. Nothing — 95% line coverage means 95% of bugs are caught; this was just bad luck.

B. Mutation testing (PIT) seeds small faults (mutants: flip conditionals, remove calls, change returns) and checks whether the suite kills them. Surviving mutants prove assertions are weak even where lines are covered — coverage measures execution, mutation measures detection.
C. Higher coverage targets — mandate 100% and the bug would have been caught.
D. More tests of the same kind; volume compensates for weak assertions.
scenarios.hint: Hint: coverage tells you the test RAN the code. What tells you the test CHECKED the code?
scenarios.why: Line coverage answers 'did this line execute?' — a test that calls the method and asserts nothing still covers every line. Mutation testing answers the harder question: 'would the suite notice if this line were wrong?' PIT generates mutants (negate a conditional, replace a return with null, drop a method call) and runs the suite against each; a mutant the suite does not kill is a hole in your assertions, pinpointed to the exact operator. The < vs <= bug is the canonical survivor: the line executes, the branch is taken, but no assertion distinguishes the boundary. 100% coverage (choice C) would not have caught it either — the line was already covered. Mutation score is the metric that measures test strength.

scenarios.title: The inverted pyramid
scenarios.situation: The suite has 3,000 end-to-end Selenium tests, 200 integration tests, and 50 unit tests. The build takes 90 minutes, tests flake constantly, and developers stopped running them locally.
evidence: Observed: The suite has 3,000 end-to-end Selenium tests, 200 integration tests, and 50 unit tests. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply the test pyramid (2) Run the TDD red-green-refactor loop Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct restructuring?
choices: A. Add more end-to-end tests — they test what users actually do, so more is better.

B. Invert toward the pyramid: many fast unit tests (milliseconds), fewer integration tests (seconds), few end-to-end tests (minutes) covering critical journeys. Fast feedback restores the local run; flakes get quarantined and fixed, not normalized.
C. Delete all tests and rely on manual QA — automated tests clearly do not work here.
D. Parallelize the 90-minute build across 100 agents; speed fixes everything.
scenarios.hint: Hint: which test level gives a developer an answer in under a second, and which one tells them 'something somewhere broke'?
scenarios.why: The test pyramid is an economic argument: unit tests cost milliseconds and pinpoint failures; integration tests cost seconds and verify wiring; E2E tests cost minutes, flake (timing, browsers, environments), and fail far from the cause. An inverted pyramid pays maximum cost for minimum diagnostic value — 90-minute feedback means nobody runs tests, so they rot, so they flake more. The fix is rebalancing: push logic down into unit-testable pure functions, keep integration tests at real boundaries (Testcontainers), and reserve E2E for a handful of critical user journeys. Parallelization (choice D) shortens the wall clock but not the flakiness or the local-run problem; it rents speed instead of fixing structure.

scenarios.title: The controller test that boots the universe
scenarios.situation: Every controller test is @SpringBootTest, booting the full context (JPA, security, messaging) in 40 seconds per class. Twenty controller classes mean 13 minutes of 'unit' testing.
evidence: Observed: Every controller test is @SpringBootTest, booting the full context (JPA, security, messaging) in 40 seconds per class. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Use Spring test slices appropriately Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Spring testing approach?
choices: A. It is fine — @SpringBootTest is the only way to test controllers.

B. Use slice tests: @WebMvcTest(controllers=...) boots only the web layer with MockMvc; mock the service layer with @MockBean. Full-context tests are reserved for a few integration slices (@DataJpaTest, @SpringBootTest smoke tests).
C. Stop testing controllers; test services only.
D. Make all controller tests static methods so Spring boots once.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what does a controller test actually need — the web layer, or the database too?
scenarios.why: @WebMvcTest loads only @Controller, @ControllerAdvice, filters, and MVC infrastructure — no JPA, no messaging, no full autoconfiguration — so the slice boots in seconds. MockMvc then drives HTTP requests against the real MVC stack (routing, serialization, validation, advice), with @MockBean standing in for the service layer. This tests exactly what a controller owns: request mapping, status codes, error bodies, validation. The full context still gets tested — by a handful of @SpringBootTest smoke tests and @DataJpaTest repository slices — but not 20 times over for every controller.

domains.name: Build Tools: Maven & Gradle
domains.description: Dependency management, multi-module builds, plugins, and reproducible CI builds with Maven and Gradle.

scenarios.title: The method that exists twice
scenarios.situation: Production throws NoSuchMethodError for a library method that exists in the source you compiled against. The dependency tree shows two versions of the same library.
evidence: Observed: Production throws NoSuchMethodError for a library method that exists in the source you compiled against. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Resolve transitive dependency conflicts (2) Use dependencyManagement and BOMs Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the fix?
choices: A. The JVM loads the wrong class file; recompile with -source 17 to fix bytecode compatibility.

B. A transitive dependency conflict: Maven's nearest-wins mediation picked an older transitive version over your direct one. Run mvn dependency:tree, add a <dependencyManagement> pin or exclusion, and verify with mvn dependency:analyze.
C. The library is corrupted; delete ~/.m2 and rebuild — that always fixes NoSuchMethodError.
D. NoSuchMethodError means the method was deleted upstream; fork the library.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the method exists in the JAR you compiled against but not in the JAR that shipped. How do two JARs get into one build?
scenarios.why: NoSuchMethodError at runtime with a clean compile is the signature of a version conflict: javac compiled against version X (with the method), but the runtime classpath resolved version Y (without it). Maven mediates conflicts with nearest-wins — the version closest to your project in the dependency graph wins, so a direct dependency usually beats a transitive one, but two competing transitives resolve by depth, not by newness. mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=... shows exactly which path won; <dependencyManagement> pins the version deterministically; exclusions cut unwanted transitives. Deleting ~/.m2 (choice C) only helps if the artifact itself is corrupt, which produces different errors.

scenarios.title: The 4-minute build that does nothing
scenarios.situation: A Gradle build takes 4 minutes even when nothing changed. Developers avoid building, so integration happens 'later' (never). The build script applies plugins in a 600-line build.gradle.
objectives: Configure incremental and cached Gradle builds
evidence: Observed: A Gradle build takes 4 minutes even when nothing changed. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Configure incremental and cached Gradle builds (2) Read a build scan Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: A. Buy faster machines — Gradle is just slow.

B. Make the build incremental and cacheable: declare task inputs/outputs correctly, enable the build cache and configuration cache, use --parallel, and split the monolith script into convention plugins; measure with build scans.
C. Delete the Gradle cache; caches always slow builds down.
D. Switch to Maven; Gradle cannot do incremental builds.
scenarios.hint: Hint: a build that 'does nothing' should do nothing — what mechanism lets Gradle skip work, and what breaks it?
scenarios.why: Gradle's speed comes from avoiding work: up-to-date checks skip tasks whose inputs/outputs are unchanged, the build cache reuses outputs across machines, and the configuration cache skips the configuration phase entirely. A 4-minute no-op build means tasks declare no inputs/outputs (so nothing is ever up-to-date), the cache is off, or configuration does expensive work on every invocation. Convention plugins (buildSrc or included builds) replace the 600-line script with composable, testable logic — and a build scan (--scan) shows exactly which tasks ran and why. Faster hardware (choice A) rents relief; deleting caches (choice C) destroys the mechanism that makes builds fast.

scenarios.title: The release that shipped mismatched modules
scenarios.situation: The release shipped api:2.4.0 with core:2.3.1 because modules were versioned and released independently. A renamed method in core broke api at runtime in production.
evidence: Observed: The release shipped api:2.4.0 with core:2.3.1 because modules were versioned and released independently. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design multi-module versioning (2) Build with the Maven/Gradle reactor Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What versioning and build discipline prevents this?
choices: A. Version and release all modules together (single version, reactor build); independent versioning is for independently deployable services, not library modules of one codebase.
B. Version each module independently but carefully — discipline solves it.
C. Merge all modules into one giant module to eliminate versioning.
D. Never rename methods; the real problem was the rename.
scenarios.hint: Hint: these modules are built from one repo and tested together — what does independent versioning buy them, and what does it cost?
scenarios.why: Library modules of one codebase are compiled and tested together — the Maven reactor (or Gradle composite) builds them in dependency order in a single run, so api can never resolve against a stale core. A single project version released atomically guarantees the artifacts in a release were built and tested together; independent versioning is designed for separately deployed services with compatibility contracts, not for modules that share a repo and a build. 'Careful' independent versioning (choice B) is a process patch over a structural problem — humans will eventually ship the mismatch again. The rename was fine; shipping untested combinations was the bug.

scenarios.title: The build that works on exactly one laptop
scenarios.situation: The build passes on the original developer's laptop and fails everywhere else: different Maven version, a plugin resolved to a newer release, and a dependency range that moved.
evidence: Observed: The build passes on the original developer's laptop and fails everywhere else: different Maven version, a plugin resolved to a newer release, and a dependency range that moved. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Pin toolchains and dependencies (2) Verify reproducibility with offline/locked builds Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a Java build reproducible?
choices: A. Document the required versions in the README and hope everyone reads it.

B. Commit the Maven/Gradle wrapper (pinned distribution), pin plugin versions, avoid version ranges, lock dependency versions, and run the identical command in CI — the build definition, not tribal knowledge, determines the toolchain.
C. Standardize on everyone's laptop having the same OS image.
D. Check in the ~/.m2 repository so everyone shares artifacts.
scenarios.hint: Hint: which files in the repo determine the exact Maven version, plugin versions, and dependency versions — and which are left to chance?
scenarios.why: Reproducibility means the build is a pure function of the repository contents: the wrapper (mvnw/gradlew) pins the exact build-tool version, plugin versions are declared (never inherited-floating), dependencies use fixed versions (no ranges like [1.0,)), and CI runs the same wrapper command on a clean agent. Version ranges and unpinned plugins make the build a function of the current date — what resolves today differs from yesterday. READMEs (choice A) describe the build; the wrapper and pins ARE the build. Checking in ~/.m2 (choice D) bloats the repo and fights every developer's local cache.

scenarios.title: The 180 MB Docker image for a 2 MB app
scenarios.situation: The service ships as a fat JAR inside a full JDK image: 180 MB, slow cold starts, and a CVE in a JDK module the app never uses. The team wants smaller, faster, safer artifacts.
objectives: Choose between fat JAR, layered, and native packaging
evidence: Observed: The service ships as a fat JAR inside a full JDK image: 180 MB, slow cold starts, and a CVE in a JDK module the app never uses. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build minimal runtimes with jlink (2) Choose between fat JAR, layered, and native packaging Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the packaging progression?
choices: A. Keep the fat JAR; image size does not matter in the cloud.

B. Layer the Docker image (dependencies vs app classes), then jlink a custom runtime with only needed modules, and consider GraalVM native images for cold-start-sensitive workloads — each step trades build complexity for size/startup/security wins.
C. Switch to a smaller base image and hope the CVE goes away.
D. Compile with -O9 for a smaller binary.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the CVE is in a module the app never loads — what packaging step removes modules the app never loads?
scenarios.why: The progression is layered: first split the Docker image so dependency layers cache (only app classes rebuild), then jlink strips the JDK to the modules your app actually uses (java.base + java.sql + ...), shrinking the runtime and removing unneeded attack surface (the CVE in an unused module disappears because the module is gone). GraalVM native-image goes further — ahead-of-time compilation to a standalone binary with millisecond startup — but demands closed-world discipline (reflection config, no dynamic class loading surprises). Each step has a cost: layering is nearly free, jlink needs module awareness, native images need reachability metadata. A smaller base image (choice C) without jlink still ships the whole JDK.

scenarios.title: The plugin that runs in the wrong phase
scenarios.situation: A code-generation plugin runs after compile, so generated sources are missing at compile time. The build worked last month. Someone 'fixed' the POM.
evidence: Observed: A code-generation plugin runs after compile, so generated sources are missing at compile time. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Diagnose Maven lifecycle issues Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined diagnosis?
choices: A. Read the effective POM (mvn help:effective-pom), find the plugin's <phase> binding, and check git blame on the POM — the lifecycle phase binding is the contract; 'worked last month' means the binding changed.
B. Reorder the plugins in the POM; Maven runs them top-to-bottom.
C. The plugin is incompatible with the JDK; upgrade everything.
D. Bind all plugins to the package phase to be safe.
scenarios.hint: Hint: Maven has two orderings — lifecycle phases, and declaration order within a phase. Which one governs?
scenarios.why: Maven executes plugins in lifecycle-phase order, not POM order (choice B is the classic misconception) — within a phase, POM order breaks ties. The effective POM (help:effective-pom) shows the merged result of parent POMs, profiles, and pluginManagement: the actual phase binding in force. git blame on the POM then names the 'fix' that moved the binding. Binding everything to package (choice D) piles ordering problems into one phase; the JDK (choice C) is unrelated to phase bindings.

domains.name: JVM Performance
domains.description: Profiling, allocation analysis, GC tuning, and JMH — making JVM applications fast on purpose.

scenarios.title: The GC tuning that changed nothing
scenarios.situation: The team spent a sprint tuning G1 flags. Pause times barely moved. Allocation profiling later showed 4 GB/s of short-lived garbage from string concatenation in a hot loop.
evidence: Observed: The team spent a sprint tuning G1 flags. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Profile allocation with JFR (2) Apply the allocation-first tuning order Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct performance order of operations?
choices: A. Keep tuning GC flags; the right combination will eventually absorb any allocation rate.

B. Reduce allocation first (the 4 GB/s is the disease; GC pauses are the symptom), then size generations, then tune the collector — measure allocation rate with JFR (jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB) before touching a single flag.
C. Increase the heap until 4 GB/s fits comfortably.
D. Switch to off-heap allocation for everything.
scenarios.hint: Hint: GC flags change how fast the truck drives. What fills the truck?
scenarios.why: GC tuning optimizes how garbage is collected; allocation profiling asks why there is so much garbage. 4 GB/s of short-lived objects saturates any collector — no flag combination makes collecting 4 GB/s cheap, because the work is proportional to allocation, not to flags. The order is fixed: profile allocation (JFR allocation events show the allocating stack traces and TLAB pressure), eliminate the garbage (StringBuilder reuse, primitive collections, object pooling where it actually helps), and only then size young gen and pick a collector for the remaining profile. A bigger heap (choice C) just delays the inevitable and lengthens full pauses; off-heap (choice D) trades GC pressure for manual memory management bugs.

scenarios.title: The benchmark that got faster when observed
scenarios.situation: A queue benchmark shows impossible throughput. Investigation finds the benchmark shares mutable state across threads without synchronization, and the 'fast' result is threads racing on a corrupted structure.
objectives: Validate benchmark results against physical bounds
evidence: Observed: A queue benchmark shows impossible throughput. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Scope JMH state correctly (2) Validate benchmark results against physical bounds Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What JMH discipline prevents this class of error?
choices: A. Benchmarks do not need thread safety; just divide the result by thread count.

B. Declare @State scopes explicitly (Benchmark vs Thread), use @Group for asymmetric workloads, isolate shared state with proper concurrency controls, and sanity-check results against a back-of-the-envelope model — impossible numbers are bugs, not victories.
C. Run with one thread; multithreaded benchmarks are meaningless.
D. Add synchronized to everything in the benchmark; correctness of the harness does not matter.
scenarios.hint: Hint: who shares the @State object, and what happens when they all mutate it at once?
scenarios.why: JMH @State(Scope.Benchmark) shares one instance across all threads — if your benchmark mutates it without synchronization, you are benchmarking a data race, and 'impossible throughput' is the race corrupting the structure into doing less work. Scope.Thread gives each thread its own state; @Group coordinates asymmetric producer/consumer benchmarks; and every result needs a plausibility check (a queue cannot exceed memory bandwidth). Single-threaded-only (choice C) abandons the actual question for concurrent structures; synchronizing the harness (choice D) measures the lock, not the structure.

scenarios.title: The premature tenuring problem
scenarios.situation: GC logs show high survivor-space overflow: short-lived request objects are promoted to old gen, which then fills and triggers long mixed collections. Young gen is 200 MB on a 8 GB heap.
evidence: Observed: GC logs show high survivor-space overflow: short-lived request objects are promoted to old gen, which then fills and triggers long mixed collections. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Size generations from GC logs (2) Diagnose premature tenuring Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct tuning response?
choices: A. Increase young generation size (and check -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold / survivor sizing) so short-lived objects die young instead of being promoted prematurely.
B. Decrease young gen further to collect more often — more frequent young GCs are always cheaper.
C. Switch to Serial GC; generational sizing does not matter there.
D. Set -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=1 to promote everything immediately and skip survivor spaces.
scenarios.hint: Hint: where SHOULD short-lived objects die, and what happens when they don't fit there?
scenarios.why: Objects that die young should never reach old gen: with a 200 MB young gen on an 8 GB heap, the eden/survivor spaces are too small for the allocation rate, so live-but-short-lived objects survive enough young collections to be tenured. Once in old gen they are expensive to reclaim (mixed/full collections) — the classic premature-tenuring pathology. The fix is sizing young gen to the application's live-set and allocation rate (often 30-50% of heap for request-driven apps) and letting MaxTenuringThreshold/survivor ratios adapt; -XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution shows the age histogram that guides the numbers. More frequent tiny young GCs (choice B) increase total GC CPU; immediate promotion (choice D) is the opposite of the fix.

scenarios.title: The synchronized map at 64 cores
scenarios.situation: A cache wrapped in synchronized methods scales to 8 cores then flatlines; at 64 cores throughput is worse than at 8. Profiling shows threads parked in monitor entry.
evidence: Observed: A cache wrapped in synchronized methods scales to 8 cores then flatlines; at 64 cores throughput is worse than at 8. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Diagnose lock contention (2) Apply the contention escalation path Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct escalation path?
choices: A. Add more cores; contention resolves with parallelism.

B. Measure first (JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter), then escalate: ConcurrentHashMap for map-shaped contention, striped locks / LongAdder for counters, and lock-free structures (queues, CAS loops) where contention is fundamental — each step removes a serialization point.
C. Replace synchronized with ReentrantLock everywhere; the lock type is the problem.
D. Shard the cache across JVMs to avoid locks entirely.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 64 threads queueing for one lock do less work than 8. What removes the queue rather than renaming it?
scenarios.why: Contention is serialization: a monitor held during cache access means 64 cores queue for one critical section, and coherence traffic makes it worse than 8 cores — adding cores (choice A) deepens the queue. The escalation is structural, not lexical: ConcurrentHashMap replaces a global lock with bin-level locking (and mostly lock-free reads); LongAdder replaces an AtomicLong hotspot with striped cells; CAS-based queues remove the lock entirely. Swapping lock types (choice C) keeps the single serialization point — ReentrantLock vs synchronized is a fairness/features choice, not a scalability fix. JFR's monitor-enter events quantify the contention in milliseconds of blocked time, which justifies each step.

scenarios.title: The allocation that never happened
scenarios.situation: JFR shows a hot method allocating thousands of Point objects per second, yet GC logs show no corresponding young-gen pressure. A teammate wants to rewrite it with object pooling.
evidence: Observed: JFR shows a hot method allocating thousands of Point objects per second, yet GC logs show no corresponding young-gen pressure. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain escape analysis (2) Verify scalar replacement before optimizing Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What should you check first?
choices: A. Nothing — the profiler is wrong; allocations always pressure the GC.

B. Whether escape analysis already eliminates the allocation: if the Point never escapes the method/thread, the JIT's scalar replacement breaks it into stack-allocated fields (or registers) — no heap allocation occurs, and pooling would add complexity for zero gain. Verify with -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis / -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations.
C. Pool the Points immediately; pooling always helps.
D. The GC logs are wrong; trust JFR and rewrite.
scenarios.hint: Hint: JFR samples where 'new' executes in bytecode. What does the JIT do with a 'new' whose result never leaves the method?
scenarios.why: The JIT performs escape analysis: if an object never escapes its allocating method (not returned, not stored in a field, not passed to unknown code), scalar replacement decomposes it into its fields held in registers or on the stack — the 'allocation' the profiler attributes never touches the heap. This is why JFR (which samples allocation sites) and GC logs (which measure heap pressure) can disagree: the allocation is real at the bytecode level and eliminated at the machine-code level. Object pooling (choice C) would reintroduce heap/shared-state complexity to 'fix' an allocation that costs nothing. Verify with -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations (debug builds) or by observing that removing the allocation changes nothing.

scenarios.title: The load test that passed and lied
scenarios.situation: Staging load tests pass at 2x expected traffic, but production falls over at 1.2x. The staging environment is identical except it runs one instance per host while production packs four.
evidence: Observed: Staging load tests pass at 2x expected traffic, but production falls over at 1.2x. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Plan capacity from production topology Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined capacity-planning response?
choices: A. The load test is wrong; increase staging traffic until it fails too.

B. Model the actual production topology: noisy-neighbor contention (CPU steal, GC interference, shared page cache) means per-instance capacity is not constant — test at production density, measure headroom per instance, and size from the bottleneck resource with a safety margin.
C. Add more instances until production survives; capacity planning is just overprovisioning.
D. Reduce production density to match staging and declare victory.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what is shared between the four instances on one host that the single staging instance had to itself?
scenarios.why: Capacity is not per-instance throughput times instance count — at 4x density, instances contend for shared host resources: CPU (steal time), memory bandwidth, disk I/O, and GC cycles that now compete with neighbors. The staging test measured an isolated instance; production runs a crowded host, so the honest test replicates production density and measures per-instance headroom under contention. Blind overprovisioning (choice C) rents ignorance expensively; matching staging density (choice D) may be right but only after measuring — it halves utilization without evidence.

scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective way to work through this bootcamp?

B. Diagnostic first: take a timed pass over scenario drills to find weak domains, study those domains' lessons with hands-on try-it exercises, drill again, then take the mock assessment under exam conditions — loop until weak areas clear.

B. Match the format: live coding -> timed try-it reps and thinking aloud; concept grilling -> Feynman explanations of the why behind each lesson; system design -> capstone-style architecture reasoning; exams -> scenario drills with careful reading of every option (distractors target real misconceptions).
C. Focus only on coding; concept questions do not matter if you can code.

scenarios.title: Designing the capstone service
scenarios.situation: You will build an order-processing service: REST API, order lifecycle, payments integration, notifications, and admin reporting. It must handle 5k concurrent users, survive restarts without losing orders, and be operable by a team that did not write it.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Design a layered service architecture; Apply the transactional outbox pattern. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What architecture satisfies these constraints?
choices: A. A single class with static methods; simplicity scales.

B. Layered Spring Boot service: controllers (REST contract) -> services (domain logic, @Transactional boundaries) -> repositories (Spring Data JPA); virtual threads for request handling; outbox pattern for reliable notifications; Actuator + Micrometer for operability; the layering makes each requirement land somewhere explicit.
C. Microservices for every entity; more services means more scalability.
D. Store everything in static HashMaps; databases are slow.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 'survive restarts without losing orders' rules out any design where the order and its side effects commit separately.
scenarios.why: Each requirement maps to an architectural decision: the layering separates the REST contract from domain logic from persistence, so each can be tested and reasoned about independently. @Transactional draws the consistency boundary (order + line items + payment intent commit atomically). Virtual threads give 5k-concurrency without reactive complexity. The transactional outbox (write the notification intent in the same transaction as the order, relay asynchronously) is what makes 'survive restarts without losing orders' actually true — dual-writes (DB + queue in one request) lose messages on crash. Actuator/Micrometer make the service operable by strangers: health, metrics, traces. Monolith-first with clean modules beats premature microservices (choice C) on every operability axis for this scale.

scenarios.title: Building it in the right order
scenarios.situation: The architecture is set. The build must proceed in an order where every step is verifiable — no 'big bang' integration at the end.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Build in vertical slices; Verify each slice independently. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What build sequence keeps every step green?
choices: A. Write all the code, then test everything at the end.

B. Vertical slices in dependency order: (1) domain model + persistence with Testcontainers tests, (2) service layer with unit tests (mocked repos), (3) REST layer with @WebMvcTest slices, (4) outbox relay with a kill -9 test, (5) virtual-thread load test, (6) Actuator/alerts — each slice demoable, each step green before the next.
C. Start with the UI; backend can follow.
D. Configure CI first, then write code to satisfy it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: after which step could you demo something to a skeptical stakeholder?
scenarios.why: Vertical slices deliver working software at every step: after step 1 you can persist orders; after step 3 you have a callable API; the outbox slice proves reliability before load testing proves scale. Each slice's tests are the right kind for its layer (Testcontainers for repos, plain unit for services, @WebMvcTest for controllers) — the testing pyramid applied per slice. Big-bang integration (choice A) discovers the wiring errors when they are most expensive; UI-first (choice C) builds on an API that does not exist yet.

scenarios.title: Shipping the capstone
scenarios.situation: The service works. Now it must be demoable by someone else and explainable in an interview: reproducible build, runnable artifact, and a writeup covering decisions and tradeoffs.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Package a runnable artifact; Document architecture decisions. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What does 'done' look like?
choices: A. 'It works on my machine' plus a verbal explanation.

B. Wrapper-pinned reproducible build, layered Docker image (or jlink runtime), docker-compose with Postgres, a README with architecture decisions + tradeoffs + how to run the kill -9 test, and a 5-minute demo script (place order -> kill -9 -> restart -> show exactly-once) — the artifact interviews for you.
C. A zip of the source directory.
D. Deploy to production; the demo is the real thing.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the interviewer will ask 'why did you choose X?' — where is that answer written down?
scenarios.why: A capstone's value is communicability: the wrapper and lockfile make the build reproducible on the interviewer's machine; the compose file makes 'run it' one command; the README's decision log (why outbox, why virtual threads, what was rejected) is what interviewers actually probe — they hire judgment, not just code. The 5-minute demo script turns reliability from a claim into theater: kill -9 mid-order, restart, show the order and exactly one notification. A source zip (choice C) is not runnable; 'works on my machine' (choice A) is not demoable.

lessons.title: Language Core — Core concepts
concepts: String literals are interned (one shared instance per distinct literal), so == can appear to work in tests, but a runtime-built string is a different object with equal content. equals() compares content — always use it for value comparison.
equals vs ==: (For null-safety, "admin".equals(input) avoids NPE.).
Integer division: promoting one operand to double before dividing (done * 100.0 / total) performs floating-point division; cast back to int for display.
Switch expressions: a switch expression is an expression: it produces a value, so no mutable accumulator is needed.

example.code:
String input = scanner.nextLine();
if (input == "admin") { grant(); }  // false for runtime strings
example.walkthrough: == on objects tests reference identity. String literals are interned (one shared instance per distinct literal), so == can appear to work in tests, but a runtime-built string is a different object with equal content. equals() compares content — always use it for value comparison.

pitfalls: Common trap: var works anywhere a type appears.
Common trap: arrow syntax only works for enums.
Common trap: switch expressions cannot have a default.
Common trap: records are syntax sugar for HashMap.

lessons.title: OOP & Design — Core concepts
concepts: @Override: without @Override, notify(Object) is just an overload — legal Java that silently does not participate in polymorphism. @Override asks the compiler to prove a matching supertype method exists; a signature mismatch becomes an error at the declaration.
Overriding equals without hashCode leaves the default identity hash, so logically-equal keys scatter across buckets and lookups miss.

Default methods narrowed the gap, but state, constructors, and single-inheritance still distinguish them. A default method provides an implementation inside the interface, so adding one does not break existing implementers — they inherit it.
Interface evolution: apply it to every intended override, including interface implementations.
Immutability: true immutability requires copying mutable inputs at construction and returning copies (or immutable views) from getters.

example.code:
public sealed interface Payment permits Card, Bank, Crypto { }
// any other implementer: compile error
example.walkthrough: sealed declares a closed set of permitted direct subtypes; anything else is a compile error. Each permitted subtype must itself be final, sealed, or non-sealed (explicit choice). Combined with pattern-matching switch, the compiler can verify exhaustiveness — adding a new payment type breaks the switch loudly instead of silently.

pitfalls: Common trap: use abstract classes whenever data is involved.
Common trap: there is no difference since Java 8 default methods.
Common trap: sealed classes cannot be implemented at all.
Common trap: mark the new method abstract and ship a migration guide.

lessons.title: Collections & Generics — Core concepts
concepts: Type erasure: generics are erased at compile time: at runtime a Cache<String> is just Cache, so the JVM could not enforce new T[]'s type safety (arrays are covariant and reified, generics are invariant and erased — the combination is unsound).
PECS: producer-extends (read from it), consumer-super (write to it — List<? super Integer> accepts Integer adds).
Producer extends: ? extends Number means 'a List of some specific subtype of Number, we know not which' — it could be List<Double>, where an Integer does not belong.

example.code:
List<String> tags = List.of("a", "b");
tags.add("c");  // UnsupportedOperationException
example.walkthrough: The List.of/Set.of/Map.of factories (Java 9+) return structurally immutable collections — any mutator throws UnsupportedOperationException. They also reject null elements outright. When callers need to mutate, copy into an ArrayList (or collect with Collectors.toList(), whose mutability is the implementation's documented choice).

pitfalls: Common trap: arrays of generics are allowed since Java 10.
Common trap: the compiler cannot verify autoboxing through wildcards.
Common trap: ? extends Number means List<Number> exactly.
Common trap: list.of returns null for empty input.

lessons.title: Streams & Lambdas — Core concepts
concepts: Lazy evaluation: (Also note orElse evaluates its argument eagerly — orElseGet takes a Supplier for lazy defaults.).
Intermediate vs terminal ops: execution is triggered by a terminal operation like forEach, collect, reduce, or count.
Effectively final: java enforces this by requiring captured locals to be final or effectively final (never reassigned).

Lambdas capture local variables by value (a copy), so allowing later mutation would create two divergent truths. A lambda that does nothing but call a method (s -> s.toUpperCase()) is exactly a method reference (String::toUpperCase).
Optional is a container signaling 'value or absence' — calling get() without checking reintroduces the exact null-dereference-style crash it replaces.
orElse vs orElseGet: the API's combinators (map, flatMap, filter, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow) handle both cases declaratively.

example.code:
Optional<User> u = repo.find(id);
return u.get().name();  // throws when empty
example.walkthrough: Optional is a container signaling 'value or absence' — calling get() without checking reintroduces the exact null-dereference-style crash it replaces. The API's combinators (map, flatMap, filter, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow) handle both cases declaratively.

pitfalls: Common trap: method references cannot take arguments.
Common trap: forEachOrdered fixes thread safety.
Common trap: wrap the collect in try/catch and retry with a HashMap.
Common trap: the pipeline needs .parallel() to run.

lessons.title: Concurrency & Virtual Threads — Core concepts
concepts: Race conditions: deadlock needs four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait).

AtomicInteger uses CAS (compare-and-set) hardware instructions to make the whole read-modify-write indivisible. (For read-modify-write like counters, volatile is not enough — that needs atomicity, i.e., AtomicInteger.).
Lost updates: hits++ compiles to load, increment, store — between any two steps another thread can interleave and its update gets overwritten (lost update).
Lock ordering: a global ordering — e.g., always lock the account with the smaller id first — makes cycles impossible.

example.code:
// thread 1: synchronized(a) { synchronized(b) { transfer(a, b); } }
// thread 2: synchronized(b) { synchronized(a) { transfer(b, a); } }  // deadlock
example.walkthrough: Deadlock needs four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait). Acquiring locks in opposite orders creates the circular wait. Alternatives: tryLock with timeout and backoff, or a single coarse lock when contention is low.

pitfalls: Common trap: virtual threads share one ThreadLocal map.
Common trap: blocking calls are forbidden on virtual threads.
Common trap: threadLocal is deprecated for virtual threads.
Common trap: virtual threads eliminate the need for executors.

lessons.title: Modules, JARs & I/O — Core concepts
concepts: JPMS: the module system (JPMS) enforces strong encapsulation: a public class in a non-exported package is inaccessible outside its module, even via reflection (without opens). exports declares the module's public API surface; everything else is implementation detail.
Executable JARs: (Fat/uber JARs additionally unpack dependencies into the single archive.).
Manifest: java -jar locates the entry point through the JAR manifest's Main-Class attribute (META-INF/MANIFEST.MF).

example.walkthrough: try-with-resources closes each resource in reverse declaration order when the block exits — normally, via return, or by exception. If both the body and close() throw, the close exception is suppressed (retrievable via getSuppressed()) rather than masking the original. Any class implementing AutoCloseable participates, including custom resources.

pitfalls: Common trap: all public classes are visible across modules.
Common trap: closeable resources are closed by the garbage collector.
Common trap: jARs cannot contain properties files.
Common trap: declare the reader outside try and close it after the catch blocks.
