lessons.title: Java — Core concepts
concepts: The JVM runs bytecode: javac compiles .java to .class, and the JVM (with its JIT compiler) executes it — 'write once, run anywhere' holds where a JVM exists. The garbage collector reclaims unreachable objects, so you manage reachability (nulling references, closing resources) rather than freeing memory.

The collections framework separates interface from implementation: List (ArrayList for random access, LinkedList for deque operations), Set (HashSet, TreeSet), Map (HashMap, TreeMap). Choosing correctly starts from the access pattern, and the equals/hashCode contract is load-bearing for every hash-based collection.

Streams express data pipelines declaratively: intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap) are lazy and fuse into a single pass; terminal operations (collect, reduce, forEach) trigger execution. Parallel streams exist but only pay off for large, CPU-bound, side-effect-free pipelines.

Concurrency uses threads, but raw Thread management is mostly obsolete: ExecutorService pools (fixed, cached, scheduled) own thread lifecycle, Futures/CompletableFuture compose async results, and java.util.concurrent provides the building blocks (ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch). Always shut down your executors.

The Java Memory Model governs cross-thread visibility: without synchronization (synchronized, volatile, locks, concurrent collections) there is no guarantee one thread sees another's writes. Immutable objects and safe publication are the simplest correct patterns.

Spring Boot is convention-over-configuration: starters pull in coherent dependency sets, auto-configuration (@ConditionalOn...) wires beans from the classpath and properties, and an embedded server (Tomcat/Jetty) means `java -jar app.jar` is the whole deployment. Externalize config per environment — never hardcode URLs or secrets.

example.walkthrough: filter is lazy — nothing runs until collect pulls elements through. groupingBy with summingDouble aggregates per order id in one pass. Records give you an immutable value type with correct equals/hashCode for free.

pitfalls: Common trap: overriding equals without hashCode — hash-based collections silently lose your entries.
Common trap: calling a stream pipeline without a terminal operation — lazy means nothing executes.
Common trap: modifying a collection during for-each iteration — fail-fast iterators throw even single-threaded.
Common trap: forgetting executor shutdown — non-daemon pool threads keep the JVM alive forever.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Java move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

concepts: Language Core is a multi-step process within Language Core: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion

Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies

lessons.title: Class Loading: Bootstrap to Application
concepts: Java's class-loader delegation model means a class loader asks its parent first, then looks in its own classpath — a class visible at compile time can be invisible at runtime if the runtime classpath or module graph differs.

Split packages (the same package in two JARs/modules) are illegal in the module system and cause silent visibility failures on the classpath; jdeps --generate-module-info and module resolution errors surface them.

Application servers and plugin frameworks create child class loaders that isolate plugins from each other — ClassNotFoundException in those environments is usually a loader-boundary problem, not a missing JAR.
The -XshowSettings:properties and -verbose:class JVM flags print exactly which class loaders load which classes from where, turning a mystery into a checklist.

example.walkthrough: This program walks the class-loader chain of the application class loader. On the module path (Java 9+) you will see AppClassLoader -> PlatformClassLoader -> null (bootstrap, implemented natively). Running with -verbose:class prints every class as it loads, prefixed by its loader — the fastest way to see which loader served a suspect class and from which JAR.

pitfalls: Assuming 'compiled fine' means 'will run fine' — compile-time and runtime classpaths are different things; provided/test-scoped Maven deps vanish at runtime.
Adding the JAR to the boot classpath (-Xbootclasspath) as a fix — it bypasses the delegation model and breaks on Java 9+ where the option is gone.
Blaming the JIT for loading errors — the JIT compiles already-loaded methods; it cannot cause ClassNotFoundException.
Recompiling everything at an older release instead of diagnosing the classpath — treats the symptom and hides split-package/module problems that will recur.
lessons.try_it: Run a small app with java -verbose:class and trace which loader loads your main class; then intentionally remove a dependency from the runtime classpath and observe the exact exception and stack.

lessons.title: Bytecode: Reading What javac Emits
concepts: Java source compiles to stack-based bytecode executed by the JVM; javap -c disassembles any class file so you can read the actual instructions.

invokedynamic links a call site at first execution through a bootstrap method, which returns a CallSite object the JVM then invokes directly — later calls go through the linked target with near-static-call performance.
Lambdas compile to invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory, so no anonymous class files are generated; method references may avoid even the indirection when they bind directly.

String concatenation (Java 9+) also uses invokedynamic with StringConcatFactory, letting the JDK evolve the concatenation strategy (MethodHandles, no more StringBuilder chains) without recompiling applications.

example.walkthrough: Disassemble any class containing a lambda with javap -c and you will see invokedynamic where an anonymous inner class used to be. The BootstrapMethods attribute names LambdaMetafactory.metafactory as the bootstrap. At first execution the bootstrap generates a hidden class implementing the functional interface and links the call site to its constructor — every later execution just instantiates it. This is why capturing vs non-capturing lambdas behave differently under the hood: non-capturing ones can reuse a singleton instance.

pitfalls: Saying lambdas are 'just syntactic sugar for anonymous classes' — since Java 8 they are invokedynamic call sites, with different performance and class-loading behavior.
Claiming invokedynamic uses reflection per call — after the one-time bootstrap linkage, invocation is a direct method-handle call, not reflective dispatch.
Reading bytecode without the BootstrapMethods table — the invokedynamic instruction alone is meaningless; the bootstrap method defines the semantics.
Assuming one lambda means one class file on disk — hidden classes are generated in memory at runtime; your JAR stays small.
lessons.try_it: Compile a class with a lambda and a method reference, run javap -c -p on it, and identify the invokedynamic instructions and their bootstrap methods in the BootstrapMethods table.

lessons.title: JIT Compilation: How Hot Code Gets Fast
concepts: The JVM interprets bytecode first and compiles hot methods later — the first iterations of any benchmark measure interpretation and compilation, not the optimized code.
Tiered compilation runs C1 (fast compile, light optimization, profiling) then C2 (slow compile, aggressive optimization using the profile); -XX:+PrintCompilation shows methods being compiled live.
Speculative optimizations (monomorphic call inlining, escape analysis scalar replacement) depend on observed behavior and can deoptimize if assumptions break — performance can change mid-run.
Dead-code elimination makes naive benchmarks measure nothing: if the result is never used, the JIT is allowed to delete the entire computation, which is why JMH's Blackhole exists.

example.walkthrough: JMH annotations declare the benchmark contract: @Warmup runs untimed iterations so the JIT reaches steady state, @Measurement collects the real samples, @Fork runs the whole thing in fresh JVMs to isolate run-to-run variance, and Blackhole.consume forces the JVM to treat the result as used, defeating dead-code elimination. Without these, you are timing the interpreter, the compiler, or literally nothing.

pitfalls: Hand-rolled timing loops with System.nanoTime and no warmup — the classic way to 'prove' the slower library is faster.
Benchmarking without consuming results — the JIT deletes dead code and you measure an empty loop.
Running all trials in one JVM without forks — profile pollution and GC state carry across trials.
Disabling tiered compilation 'for consistency' — you then measure a configuration nobody runs in production.
lessons.try_it: Write a JMH benchmark comparing ArrayList vs LinkedList random access, run it, and explain the assembly-free result in terms of cache locality rather than big-O.

lessons.title: Garbage Collectors: Choosing G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah
concepts: Throughput collectors (Parallel) maximize work done per CPU second but pause the world for whole-heap collections — ideal for batch jobs, wrong for latency SLAs.
Low-pause collectors (ZGC, Shenandoah) do marking and relocation concurrently with the application, keeping pauses in the single-digit milliseconds on heaps from gigabytes to terabytes.
G1 is the balanced default: regional heap, concurrent marking, mixed collections that bound pause time toward -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (a goal, not a guarantee).
GC logs (-Xlog:gc*) are the ground truth: allocation rate, live-set size, and pause phases tell you which collector fits instead of guessing.

example.code:
# Switch a latency-sensitive service to ZGC and log what happens
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms16g -Xmx16g \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags \
     -jar trading-service.jar
# Then check: grep "Pause" gc.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort -n | tail
example.walkthrough: This launches the service on ZGC with structured GC logging. ZGC reports every pause phase with microsecond precision, so grepping the log shows the actual pause distribution to compare against the 20 ms SLA. The fixed 16 GB heap (-Xms = -Xmx) avoids resize pauses, and the log file becomes the evidence for whether the collector switch actually fixed p99 — never trust a GC change without before/after pause histograms.

pitfalls: Doubling the heap to 'fix' pauses on a throughput collector — full GC pause scales with live data, so this usually makes the worst pauses longer.
Choosing Serial GC for latency — single-threaded full collections on a 16 GB heap produce multi-second pauses.
Running Epsilon in production — it allocates until the heap is exhausted and then throws OutOfMemoryError by design.
Changing collectors without GC logs — you cannot tune what you do not measure; every collector change needs before/after pause data.
lessons.try_it: Enable GC logging on any local Java app, force some allocation, and identify young-gen vs old-gen collections and their pause times in the log.

lessons.title: JVM Memory Areas: Heap, Metaspace, and Native Memory
concepts: The JVM process memory = heap (-Xmx) + Metaspace + thread stacks + code cache + direct buffers + GC/JVM native structures; containers OOM-kill on the total, not the heap.

Metaspace holds class metadata and is unbounded by default — dynamic class generation (proxies, scripting engines, repeated redeploys) leaks it, and -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize plus class-unloading analysis bounds it.
Each platform thread reserves a stack (default 1 MB virtual, committed lazily); thread-per-request architectures with thousands of threads are a native-memory problem that virtual threads solve.
Native Memory Tracking (jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory detail) breaks down off-heap usage by category, turning 'mystery OOM' into an itemized bill.

example.code:
# Diagnose off-heap growth on a running JVM
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory detail
# Key sections: Java Heap (capped by -Xmx), Class (Metaspace),
# Thread (stacks = thread count x -Xss), Internal (direct buffers),
# Code (JIT code cache)
example.walkthrough: jcmd attaches to the running JVM and dumps NMT categories with committed vs reserved bytes. Compare two snapshots an hour apart: growth in 'Class' means class-metadata leak, growth in 'Thread' means thread leak, growth in 'Internal' means direct-buffer leak. This is the diagnostic that separates 'increase -Xmx' (wrong when heap is healthy) from the real fix — capping the category that is actually growing.

pitfalls: Raising -Xmx when heap metrics are healthy — the OOM is off-heap; a bigger heap leaves even less room for native memory inside the container.
Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit — guarantees OOM kills, since Metaspace, stacks, and code cache need hundreds of MB beyond the heap.
Ignoring thread count — 2,000 platform threads at 1 MB stacks is 2 GB of virtual address space before a single object is allocated.
Upgrading Java 'to fix container support' on Java 11+ — container awareness (-XX:+UseContainerSupport) has been default since Java 10; the problem is measurement, not the version.
lessons.try_it: Run any Java app with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=detail, take two jcmd VM.native_memory snapshots, and identify the largest non-heap categories.

lessons.title: Autoconfiguration: How Spring Boot Decides for You
concepts: @ConditionalOnClass / @ConditionalOnMissingBean / @ConditionalOnProperty are the decision points — autoconfiguration is a set of if-statements evaluated at startup, readable in the condition evaluation report (--debug).
Starter POMs are curated dependency sets (spring-boot-starter-web pulls Tomcat + Jackson + validation); they exist so the classpath conditions have something to react to.
@SpringBootApplication bundles @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan — exclude specific auto-configs with exclude = {...} when they fight your setup.
The --debug flag (or logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG) prints the full condition evaluation report: which auto-configs matched, which did not, and why.

example.walkthrough: Running with spring-boot-starter-data-jpa on the classpath and spring.datasource.url set, the context contains a HikariDataSource created by DataSourceAutoConfiguration — no @Bean method written by hand. Add your own @Bean DataSource method and re-run: the auto-config backs off (@ConditionalOnMissingBean) and yours wins. Run once with --debug to see the condition evaluation report listing DataSourceAutoConfiguration as matched and the reason.

pitfalls: Assuming autoconfiguration is magic that cannot be inspected — the condition evaluation report (--debug) shows every decision.
Defining a bean and being surprised the auto-config still applies — check the condition: some auto-configs use @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate or property flags, not OnMissingBean.
Excluding the wrong auto-config to fix a conflict — exclude narrowly and verify with the report rather than disabling whole groups.
Putting @ComponentScan on everything to 'find' beans — component scanning finds YOUR classes; auto-configs come from spring.factories regardless of scan packages.
lessons.try_it: Create a fresh Spring Boot app, run it with --debug, and find DataSourceAutoConfiguration (or its absence) in the condition evaluation report; then add a custom DataSource @Bean and watch it back off.

lessons.title: Dependency Injection: Constructor Injection and Bean Scopes
concepts: Constructor injection expresses required dependencies as final fields set once at construction — the object is always valid, and the wiring is visible in the signature.
Field injection requires the container (or reflection) to populate private fields, making the class untestable in isolation and hiding its real collaborators.

Bean scopes interact with injection: injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton needs a scoped proxy, otherwise the singleton holds a stale instance — constructor injection surfaces this at startup.
Circular dependencies are a design smell that constructor injection exposes immediately (BeanCurrentlyInCreationException) while field injection silently allows via proxies.

example.walkthrough: Two final fields, one constructor, no annotations on the fields (Spring autowires the single constructor implicitly). In production the container resolves OrderRepository and Clock beans; in a unit test you pass a Mockito mock and Clock.fixed(...) directly — the class under test has zero framework coupling. Compare with field injection, where the same test would need @SpringBootTest or ReflectionTestUtils.setField — both slower and more brittle.

pitfalls: Using field injection 'because it is less code' — the saved lines cost you testability and explicit wiring; constructor injection is the team standard for a reason.
Adding @Autowired to the constructor unnecessarily — a single constructor is autowired implicitly since Spring 4.3; the annotation is noise.
Injecting request/session-scoped beans into singletons without proxies — the singleton captures the first request's instance; use scoped proxies or ObjectProvider.
Hiding circular dependencies with setter/field injection — the cycle is still there; constructor injection forces you to break it properly (events, refactoring).
lessons.try_it: Refactor one field-injected service in a sample app to constructor injection, then write a plain JUnit test (no Spring annotations) that constructs it with mocks.

lessons.title: REST Controllers: Status Codes, Validation, and Error Bodies
concepts: Status codes are infrastructure-readable: 4xx means the client can fix and retry differently, 5xx means the server failed; caches, retries, and alerts all key off them.
@ControllerAdvice centralizes exception-to-response mapping — one place defines the error contract instead of try/catch in every controller.
Bean Validation annotations (@NotBlank, @Positive, @Valid for nested) on DTOs plus a MethodArgumentNotValidException handler produce consistent 400s with field-level details.
POST for creation should return 201 with a Location header; idempotent updates use PUT; partial updates use PATCH — method semantics are part of the contract.

example.walkthrough: The controller expresses the happy path only; the missing-order case throws a domain exception. A @ControllerAdvice class catches OrderNotFoundException and builds a 404 response with an RFC 7807 body — the controller never touches HTTP error plumbing. Add @Valid to a @RequestBody DTO parameter and invalid payloads become 400s automatically. This separation is what keeps controllers thin and error contracts consistent across dozens of endpoints.

pitfalls: Returning 200 with an error payload — breaks caching, retry logic, monitoring, and every HTTP-aware tool in the chain.
Scattering try/catch and ResponseEntity.status(...) through controllers — the error contract drifts per endpoint; centralize with @ControllerAdvice.
Validating in service code instead of at the boundary — duplicates checks and lets invalid data travel deeper than it should.
Exposing stack traces or internal messages in error bodies — leaks implementation details; log them server-side, return stable codes to clients.
lessons.try_it: Build a tiny controller with a @ControllerAdvice handler and verify with curl that a missing resource returns 404 with a JSON problem body, and that an invalid @Valid DTO returns 400.

lessons.title: Spring Data JPA: Repositories, Queries, and the N+1 Trap
concepts: Lazy associations load on first access — convenient in a transaction, catastrophic when a serializer walks the graph outside one (or inside, N times).
@EntityGraph and JOIN FETCH convert N+1 into 1+0 by fetching the association in the original query; DTO projections go further by selecting only needed columns.
Derived query methods (findByStatusOrderByCreatedDesc) are parsed into JPQL — powerful, but complex fetches deserve explicit @Query where the SQL is visible and reviewable.
Open Session in View hides LazyInitializationException by keeping the session open through rendering — it masks the N+1 instead of fixing it and holds connections during view rendering.

example.walkthrough: Both variants load orders and their line items in a single SQL statement with a join. @EntityGraph is declarative and composes with derived queries; the explicit @Query makes the fetch strategy visible in code review. Verify with spring.jpa.show-sql or a query counter in tests: the endpoint should emit a constant number of queries regardless of row count — that constancy is the acceptance test for the fix.

pitfalls: Serializing JPA entities directly to JSON — lazy loading, bidirectional references (infinite recursion), and N+1 all follow; map to DTOs at the service boundary.
Leaving Open Session in View enabled to silence LazyInitializationException — it papers over N+1 and ties connection lifetime to view rendering.
Fetching everything eagerly 'to be safe' — EAGER on collections causes Cartesian products and loads data no caller needs; default to LAZY and fetch explicitly.
Writing the fix without a query-count test — N+1 regressions return silently; assert query counts in integration tests.
lessons.try_it: Write a test that counts SQL statements for an endpoint (e.g. via a datasource proxy), reproduce N+1 with lazy loading, then fix it with @EntityGraph and watch the count go constant.

lessons.title: Actuator, Metrics, and Production Observability
concepts: Liveness vs readiness: liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure removes it from rotation — a saturated pool should fail readiness, not liveness, to avoid restart loops.
Micrometer + Actuator expose JVM, pool, and HTTP metrics in Prometheus/OpenTelemetry formats; custom business metrics (orders_placed_total) ride the same pipeline.
Distributed tracing (Micrometer Tracing / OpenTelemetry) propagates trace IDs across service calls — the 20-minute outage becomes one trace showing exactly where requests queued.
Expose only what operations needs: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus — never dump env or heapdumps unauthenticated.

example.code:
# application.properties — production-ready actuator
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when_authorized
management.health.db.enabled=true
# Kubernetes probes:
# liveness:  /actuator/health/liveness
# readiness: /actuator/health/readiness
example.walkthrough: This exposes health plus Prometheus-scrapable metrics while keeping sensitive endpoints (env, heapdump) closed. show-details=when_authorized gives operators full health detail without leaking it publicly. Kubernetes probes hit the liveness/readiness groups separately: a saturated DB pool flips readiness (traffic drains, instance recovers) instead of triggering a restart loop. Pair with an alert on hikaricp_connections_pending > 0 — pending threads mean the pool is the bottleneck, minutes before the outage.

pitfalls: Health-checking / instead of /actuator/health — the web layer can serve 200 while every downstream dependency is dead.
Exposing all actuator endpoints publicly — /actuator/env leaks secrets and /actuator/heapdump is a DoS vector; restrict exposure and secure with when_authorized.
Alerting on CPU only — pool exhaustion, thread starvation, and latency percentiles are the signals that precede Java service outages.
No tracing across services — without trace IDs, a 20-minute outage is twenty minutes of grepping disjoint logs.
lessons.try_it: Enable Actuator on a sample app, hit /actuator/health and /actuator/metrics, then saturate a tiny Hikari pool and watch the pool metrics move.

lessons.title: JUnit 5: Assertions, Lifecycle, and Parameterized Tests
concepts: @ParameterizedTest separates test logic from test data — the method is written once, rows are data, and failures name the exact row.
@MethodSource (a static Stream<Arguments> factory) handles complex inputs; @CsvSource covers scalars inline; @EnumSource exhausts enums — pick the source that fits the data shape.
Lifecycle annotations (@BeforeEach, @AfterEach) run per case, so parameterized cases stay isolated — shared mutable fixtures across rows are the new copy-paste bug.
AssertJ/assertions with descriptive messages beat bare assertEquals: assertThat(tax).as("bracket %s", bracket).isEqualTo(expected) tells you which row failed and why.

example.walkthrough: Each CSV row becomes an independent test case with a readable name ('income 50000 -> tax 5000'). Adding a bracket is adding a row — no new method, no copy-paste, no silent typo. The name pattern interpolates arguments so the test report reads like a specification. For richer inputs (objects, lists), swap @CsvSource for a @MethodSource returning Stream<Arguments>.

pitfalls: Copy-pasting test methods per input — duplication rots; one typo'd copy fails (or worse, passes vacuously) for months.
Sharing mutable state between parameterized rows — @BeforeEach must reset fixtures or rows interfere.
Using @ValueSource for multi-argument cases — it only supplies one argument per row; reach for @CsvSource or @MethodSource.
Vague assertion messages — when row 37 of 40 fails, assertThat(...).as("bracket %s", input) is the difference between a 5-second and a 30-minute diagnosis.
lessons.try_it: Convert any 3+ copy-pasted test methods you have into one @ParameterizedTest with @CsvSource and named cases.

lessons.title: Mockito: Stubs, Verification, and What Not to Mock
concepts: Mock collaborators, not the unit: the class under test is always real; its dependencies (repositories, clients, clocks) are the mock candidates.

Stub queries, verify commands: stubbing answers 'what does the dependency return?', verify() answers 'did the unit send the right command?' — over-verifying every call couples tests to implementation.
Prefer lenient, behavior-focused stubs: strict stubbing (Mockito's default strictness) fails on unused stubs, which catches tests that drift from the code they claim to cover.
Do not mock what you do not own AND can avoid: wrap third-party APIs behind your own interface, then mock the interface — your tests survive library upgrades.

example.walkthrough: The service is real — constructed with a mocked repository and a fixed clock. The test stubs the query (findById returns the order), invokes the real cancel logic, asserts the resulting state, and verifies the save command went out. If cancel() is later refactored to use a different repository method, the stub fails loudly (strict stubs) instead of silently passing — the test stays honest about what the code actually does.

pitfalls: Mocking the class under test — asserts against your own stubs; passes with any (or no) implementation.
verify() on every interaction — overspecified tests break on harmless refactors; verify commands and outcomes, not internal chatter.
Mocking value objects, entities, and JDK types — brittle, unreadable, and pointless; use real ones.
Stubbing with any() matchers everywhere — the test stops specifying behavior and passes for inputs the code never handles.
lessons.try_it: Find a test in a sample project that mocks the class under test (or over-verifies), rewrite it with the real object and mocked boundaries, and compare readability.

lessons.title: Testcontainers: Real Dependencies in Integration Tests
concepts: Test against real dependencies: Testcontainers provisions Dockerized Postgres/Kafka/Redis per test class or suite, so dialect, types, and semantics match production.
@DynamicPropertySource (or @ServiceConnection in Spring Boot 3.1+) wires the container's mapped port into the app config — no hardcoded ports, no test-specific properties files.
Container reuse strategies (singleton containers, reusable=true) keep suite time sane; startup cost is paid once per suite, not per test.
Keep the pyramid: Testcontainers for repository/integration slices, not for every unit test — spinning Postgres to test a pure function is waste.

example.walkthrough: The container starts once per test class (static field), and @DynamicPropertySource injects its actual JDBC URL into the Spring environment before the context boots. Every repository test now executes against genuine Postgres 16: the dialect-specific function either works or fails here, in CI, before merge. Spring Boot 3.1+ simplifies further with @ServiceConnection on the container field — no @DynamicPropertySource needed.

pitfalls: Testing against H2 and calling it Postgres coverage — dialect differences make the green build a lie.
Hardcoding container ports in test properties — parallel builds collide; use dynamic property injection.
One container per test method — startup time explodes; scope containers per class or suite.
Forgetting Docker in CI — Testcontainers needs a Docker daemon; the 'works locally, fails in CI' inverse happens when the pipeline lacks it.
lessons.try_it: Convert one H2-based repository test to Testcontainers Postgres and watch a dialect-specific behavior (e.g. ILIKE, jsonb, case sensitivity) get tested for real.

lessons.title: Mutation Testing: Are Your Tests Actually Checking?
concepts: Line/branch coverage measures execution; mutation score measures fault detection — a suite can be 100% covered and still assert nothing.
PIT (pitest) integrates with Maven/Gradle and JUnit 5, mutating bytecode operators (conditionals, increments, returns, void calls) and reporting surviving mutants per class.
Equivalent mutants (changes no test could detect, e.g. reordering side-effect-free calls) are noise — triage survivors, don't chase 100% mutation score blindly.
Target mutation testing at critical code first (billing, auth, safety logic): full-suite mutation runs are slow, so scope to what matters and run in CI nightly.

example.code:
<!-- Maven: PIT with JUnit 5 -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.pitest</groupId>
  <artifactId>pitest-maven</artifactId>
  <version>1.15.0</version>
  <configuration>
    <targetClasses><param>com.shop.billing.*</param></targetClasses>
    <targetTests><param>com.shop.billing.*</param></targetTests>
    <mutators><mutator>CONDITIONALS_BOUNDARY</mutator></mutators>
  </configuration>
</plugin>
example.walkthrough: CONDITIONALS_BOUNDARY is the mutator that flips < to <= and friends — exactly the production bug class. Scoped to the billing package, PIT runs the package's tests against each mutant and reports survivors. A surviving boundary mutant names the test file and the assertion to strengthen. Run the default mutator set first for breadth, then boundary mutators on critical packages for depth.

pitfalls: Treating 95% coverage as 'tested' — coverage without assertions is a vanity metric; mutation score is the audit.
Running mutation testing on the whole codebase every commit — too slow; scope to changed/critical code in PRs and full runs nightly.
Chasing 100% mutation score including equivalent mutants — some mutants are semantically identical; kill the meaningful ones.
Adding more assertion-free tests to raise coverage — volume without oracles just makes the suite slower, not stronger.
lessons.try_it: Run PIT on one package of a sample project with CONDITIONALS_BOUNDARY, pick a surviving mutant, and strengthen the test until it dies.

lessons.title: TDD and the Test Pyramid in Practice
concepts: The pyramid: 70/20/10-ish split across unit/integration/E2E — fast, deterministic tests at the base; slow, flaky, high-value-journey tests at the tip.
TDD's real benefit is design feedback: writing the test first forces small, injectable, single-purpose units — the testability pressure shapes the production code.
Flaky tests are bugs, not weather: quarantine on first flake, fix or delete within the sprint — a suite developers distrust is a suite that gets ignored.
The local loop is the contract: the full unit suite must run in seconds on a laptop, or developers will not run it, and unrun tests are unwritten tests.

example.walkthrough: Red: the test names the behavior before the code exists, and fails for the right reason. Green: the smallest change that passes — no gold-plating. Refactor: with the test as a safety net, extract the discount policy into its own object. The loop's output is not just tested code but code shaped by testability — small units with explicit dependencies.

pitfalls: Writing all tests after the code as a separate phase — you get coverage theater without the design pressure TDD provides.
Normalizing flaky tests ('just re-run') — flakiness compounds until the suite is noise; quarantine and fix.
Testing through the UI what a unit test could check — slow, brittle, and diagnostically useless when it fails.
Skipping the refactor step — red-green without refactor accumulates test-induced design damage; the third step is not optional.
lessons.try_it: Take one untested pure function, write the test first (watch it fail), implement minimally, then refactor — and time how long the whole loop takes.

lessons.title: Maven: Coordinates, Scopes, and the Dependency Tree
concepts: Maven coordinates (groupId:artifactId:version) plus scope (compile/provided/runtime/test) fully determine what ships; provided and test scopes vanish from the runtime artifact.
Nearest-wins mediation: on conflict, the dependency nearest your POM in the graph wins — declare contested libraries directly or pin them in <dependencyManagement>.
mvn dependency:tree reveals the winning version and the losing paths; mvn dependency:analyze flags used-but-undeclared and declared-but-unused dependencies.
Bills of materials (BOMs, e.g. spring-boot-dependencies) pin dozens of versions coherently — import one instead of hand-pinning twenty libraries.

example.code:
<!-- Pin the version once, deterministically -->
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
      <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
      <version>2.17.1</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
example.walkthrough: Every module (and every transitive path) now resolves jackson-databind to 2.17.1 regardless of what any library requests — the conflict is decided in one visible place instead of by graph depth. Pair with mvn dependency:tree in CI to fail the build when unexpected duplicates appear; the tree is the contract, the management section is the enforcement.

pitfalls: Letting transitive versions float — builds become non-reproducible and NoSuchMethodError appears on the worst possible day.
Adding exclusions one by one instead of a dependencyManagement pin — whack-a-mole across modules; pin once at the parent.
Declaring provided-scope deps and shipping without them — provided means 'the container supplies it'; in a fat JAR nothing supplies it.
Ignoring dependency:analyze warnings — used-undeclared deps break the moment the transitive path that smuggled them changes.
lessons.try_it: Run mvn dependency:tree on a sample project, find a library appearing twice, and pin it in dependencyManagement; verify the tree shows one version.

lessons.title: Gradle: Build Scripts, Configuration Cache, and Task Graph
concepts: Incremental build: tasks with declared inputs/outputs are skipped when nothing changed — undeclared inputs (System.getenv reads, absolute paths) silently break up-to-dateness.
Build cache (local + remote) reuses task outputs across checkouts and CI agents; configuration cache reuses the configured task graph — together they make no-op builds take seconds.
Convention plugins package shared build logic (Java versions, test config, publishing) as reusable plugins instead of copy-pasted script blocks.
Build scans profile the build itself: task execution timeline, cache hit rates, and configuration time — the profiler for your build.

example.walkthrough: Caching, parallel execution, and the configuration cache attack the three phases: execution (skip/reuse), task graph (parallel), and configuration (skip entirely). Run the build twice with --scan: the second scan should show most tasks FROM-CACHE or UP-TO-DATE and near-zero configuration time. Any task that still runs on the no-op build is misconfigured — its inputs/outputs are the bug.

pitfalls: Tasks without declared inputs/outputs — Gradle can never skip them, so every build is a full build.
Reading environment state in configuration phase — breaks the configuration cache and makes builds order-dependent.
One giant build.gradle for everything — untestable, unshareable; extract convention plugins.
Tuning without a build scan — guessing at build performance instead of measuring which phase dominates.
lessons.try_it: Enable the three properties on a sample Gradle build, run twice with --scan, and identify which tasks still execute on the no-op run and why.

lessons.title: Multi-Module Builds and Versioning Strategy
concepts: Reactor builds compile modules in dependency order in one invocation — inter-module deps resolve to the just-built classes, never to stale repository artifacts.
Single-version multi-module releases are atomic: every artifact in 2.4.0 was built and tested together, so runtime combinations are always the tested ones.
Independent versioning belongs to independently deployed units (services, published libraries) with explicit compatibility ranges — not to modules of one application.
CI should build the full reactor on every change (or use -pl with -am to include dependencies); testing api against yesterday's core is testing a combination that will never ship.

example.code:
<!-- parent POM: one version for the reactor -->
<groupId>com.shop</groupId>
<artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
<version>2.4.0</version>
<packaging>pom</packaging>
<modules>
  <module>shop-core</module>
  <module>shop-api</module>
</modules>
example.walkthrough: One version, one reactor, one release: mvn release:prepare/release:perform (or the Gradle equivalent) tags and publishes every module at 2.4.0 together. shop-api's dependency on shop-core resolves within the reactor to the current sources — the renamed method breaks the build at compile time, in CI, before any release exists. The failure moves from 'production runtime' to 'pull request', which is the entire point.

pitfalls: Independently versioning modules of one application — eventually ships an untested combination; the mismatch in the scenario is the predictable outcome.
Building modules in isolation in CI (-pl without -am) — tests a combination that never ships and misses cross-module breakage.
Publishing SNAPSHOTs that downstream modules consume — non-reproducible builds where 'it worked yesterday' is literally true and useless.
Merging everything into one module to dodge versioning — trades a solved problem for an unbuildable monolith; keep modules, unify the version.
lessons.try_it: Convert a sample project's independently-versioned modules to a single-version reactor and verify that a cross-module rename fails the build instead of shipping.

lessons.title: Reproducible Builds: Locking, Wrappers, and CI
concepts: Wrappers (mvnw, gradlew) pin the build tool version in the repo — 'works on my machine' starts with different build tools, and the wrapper eliminates that class.
Pin everything: plugin versions in <build><plugins>, dependency versions fixed (no LATEST, no ranges) — floating versions make builds time-dependent.
Lockfiles (Gradle dependency locking, Maven's reproducible-build plugins) record the exact resolved graph; CI verifies against the lock instead of re-resolving.
CI builds from a clean checkout with the wrapper command — if it is not built in CI from scratch, it is not reproducible, whatever laptops do.

example.code:
# The reproducibility checklist, as commands
./mvnw -v            # pinned Maven version, from the repo
./mvnw -o clean verify # offline: proves no undeclared network deps
# gradle: ./gradlew dependencies --write-locks  (lockfile committed)
example.walkthrough: mvnw -v prints the wrapper-pinned Maven version — identical on every machine. The offline build (-o) is the acid test: if the build needs the network for anything but declared repositories, something is unpinned. Gradle's --write-locks records the resolved graph; CI then builds with --locked, failing if the graph drifts. Together: same tool, same inputs, same outputs, anywhere.

pitfalls: Version ranges in dependencies ([1.2,2.0)) — the build resolves differently over time; today's green build is tomorrow's conflict.
Unpinned plugin versions — Maven warns and picks; what it picks changes with releases.
README-driven toolchain setup — tribal knowledge rots; the wrapper is the executable documentation.
Skipping the clean CI build — incremental local state hides missing declarations until release day.
lessons.try_it: Take a sample build, add the wrapper if missing, pin one floating version, and prove the offline build passes.

lessons.title: Fat JARs, jlink, and Native Images
concepts: Layered Docker images separate dependencies (rarely change) from app classes (change every build) — pulls and rebuilds touch only the top layer.
jlink --add-modules builds a runtime image containing only the modules your app needs — smaller image, smaller attack surface, faster startup than a full JDK.
GraalVM native-image compiles to a self-contained binary: near-instant startup and tiny RSS, at the cost of closed-world constraints (reflection/resource configuration).
The module path (vs classpath) is what makes jlink possible — unnamed-module fat JARs cannot be jlinked; modularize or accept the full JDK.

example.code:
# Custom runtime with only what the app needs
jdeps --print-module-deps target/app.jar   # -> java.base,java.sql,...
jlink --add-modules java.base,java.sql \
      --output custom-runtime --compress=2
# Docker: FROM scratch-ish + custom-runtime + app classes
example.walkthrough: jdeps computes the exact module closure from your JAR; jlink assembles a runtime with only those modules, compressed. The resulting image drops from ~300 MB (full JDK) to tens of MB, cold start improves (less to initialize), and the CVE in the unused desktop module is gone — the module is not in the image. For Spring Boot apps, layered jars (layertools) achieve the Docker-layering step without restructuring the build.

pitfalls: Shipping the full JDK 'because it is simpler' — you ship CVEs in modules you never execute and pay the size on every deploy.
jlink on a classpath-based fat JAR — jlink needs modules; run jdeps first and modularize (or use automatic modules) deliberately.
Native-image without reflection config — dynamic proxies and reflection fail at runtime with cryptic errors; generate metadata with the tracing agent.
Optimizing image size while ignoring layer caching — a small image that rebuilds fully every deploy is slower to ship than a larger well-layered one.
lessons.try_it: Run jdeps on a sample JAR, build a jlink runtime with its module closure, and compare image sizes.

lessons.title: Allocation Profiling: Finding Garbage Before Tuning GC
concepts: Allocation rate (GB/s) is the primary metric — it bounds what any collector can achieve; measure it before tuning anything.
JFR's jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB / OutsideTLAB events attribute allocation to exact stack traces — the profile names the code to fix, not the flag to flip.
Most allocation sins are mundane: string concatenation in loops, autoboxing in hot paths, Optional/stream chains allocating per element, oversized default collection capacities.
Escape analysis already eliminates many allocations (scalar replacement) — verify with -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis before hand-optimizing what the JIT already removes.

example.walkthrough: Two minutes of JFR on the production-shaped workload, opened in Mission Control, ranks allocating stack traces by bytes. The top entry is the 4 GB/s — typically a toString/concatenation in a loop or a per-request object graph. Fixing it (reused StringBuilder, primitive specialization, right-sized collections) cuts allocation at the source; re-run JFR to confirm the rate dropped before ever touching GC flags.

pitfalls: Tuning GC flags before measuring allocation — optimizing the symptom while the disease (allocation rate) is unbounded.
Micro-optimizing allocations the JIT already eliminates — check escape analysis before rewriting clean code into ugly fast-looking code.
Pooling everything — object pools add concurrency bugs and often lose to TLAB allocation (which costs ~10 CPU cycles); pool only expensive resources (connections, buffers).
Benchmarking allocation fixes with a cold JVM — allocation behavior changes after warmup; measure at steady state.
lessons.try_it: Run a 2-minute JFR allocation profile on any Java workload and identify the top allocating stack trace; estimate its GB/s.

lessons.title: JMH Beyond Basics: State, Forks, and False Sharing
concepts: @State(Scope.Benchmark) = shared across threads; Scope.Thread = per-thread; Scope.Group = per group — the scope declares the concurrency contract of your fixture.
Shared mutable benchmark state must use the same concurrency discipline as production code, or the benchmark measures a race instead of the structure.
@Group with @GroupThreads models asymmetric workloads (readers vs writers); without it you benchmark a workload that never occurs.
Sanity-check against physics: throughput above memory bandwidth, latency below a cache miss, or scaling above core count means the harness is broken — investigate, don't celebrate.

example.walkthrough: Scope.Thread gives every worker thread its own queue — the benchmark measures single-threaded offer/poll with zero contention, honestly. To measure contention, switch to Scope.Benchmark with a properly concurrent queue and multiple @Threads — now the sharing is deliberate and the structure under test is actually thread-safe. The scope annotation is the difference between 'benchmarking a race' and 'benchmarking concurrency'.

pitfalls: Scope.Benchmark with unsynchronized mutable state — the classic impossible-throughput bug; threads corrupt the fixture and do less work.
Celebrating impossible numbers — if the result beats a back-of-the-envelope bound, the harness is wrong; fast wrong answers are still wrong.
Benchmarking with @GroupThreads but one @State — asymmetric threads need their coordination declared, not assumed.
Ignoring JMH's -prof gc/stack profilers — they attribute allocation and hotspots inside the benchmark, catching fixture costs disguised as structure costs.
lessons.try_it: Write a JMH benchmark with Scope.Thread state, then deliberately switch to shared unsynchronized state and observe the 'impossible' result — then explain why.

lessons.title: GC Tuning in Practice: Sizing Generations
concepts: Generational hypothesis: most objects die young — size eden so the young die in young gen, and old gen holds only the genuinely long-lived.
Premature tenuring (survivor overflow) shows in GC logs as high desired-survivor-size pressure and young objects appearing in old gen — the fix is bigger young gen, not a different collector.
-XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution (or JFR jdk.GCHeapSummary) shows object age histograms — tune thresholds from the histogram, not from folklore.
G1's -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis is a goal the collector works toward by sizing young gen dynamically — set it, then verify pauses in logs instead of hand-sizing every region.

example.code:
# Diagnose tenuring pressure from GC logs
java -Xlog:gc*,gc+age=trace:file=gc.log:time,level,tags -jar app.jar
# Look for: 'Desired survivor size', age table distribution,
# and promotion rates into old gen per young GC
example.walkthrough: gc+age=trace logs the per-age object distribution at each young collection — the age table shows exactly how many bytes survive to each age and what gets promoted. If most promotion happens at age 1-2 with a small desired survivor size, young gen is undersized for the allocation rate: grow it (e.g. -Xmn or G1's NewSize) and re-measure. The log, not a blog post's flags, is the tuning input.

pitfalls: Copying another app's GC flags — tenuring behavior depends on YOUR allocation rate and live set; flags are not transferable.
Setting MaxTenuringThreshold=1 'to reduce copying' — promotes everything, filling old gen with garbage that dies expensively.
Shrinking young gen to 'collect faster' — increases promotion rate and total GC CPU; young GCs are cheap precisely because most objects are already dead.
Tuning without gc+age logs — flying blind on the single most informative diagnostic for generational sizing.
lessons.try_it: Enable gc+age logging on a sample app, read the age table, and explain where the application's objects die.

lessons.title: Lock Contention and the Path to Lock-Free
concepts: Contention serializes parallel hardware: measure blocked time (JFR JavaMonitorEnter, async-profiler wall mode) before restructuring — not all slowness is contention.
ConcurrentHashMap: lock-free reads, bin-level locks on write — the default answer for map-shaped shared state; computeIfAbsent is atomic per bin.
Striping (LongAdder, striped locks) trades read-aggregation cost for write scalability — right for counters and hot keys, wrong for strongly consistent reads.
Lock-free (CAS loops, concurrent queues) removes the serialization point entirely but demands careful reasoning about ABA, retries, and progress guarantees.

example.walkthrough: computeIfAbsent is atomic per hash bin: two threads loading different keys proceed in parallel, and same-key races resolve to a single load. The global monitor is gone — 64 cores now scale with the key distribution instead of queueing on one lock. JFR before/after shows monitor-enter blocked time collapsing; throughput scales until the next bottleneck (often the loader itself), which is progress.

pitfalls: Replacing synchronized with ReentrantLock and declaring victory — same serialization point, different API; scalability is unchanged.
Striping without understanding read costs — LongAdder.sum() is O(cells); reading a striped counter in a hot loop can cost more than it saved.
Lock-free everywhere by default — CAS retry storms under extreme contention can outperform locks or collapse; measure, and prefer structured concurrency (ConcurrentHashMap) first.
Sharding across JVMs before fixing in-process contention — distributed complexity to dodge a data-structure choice; fix the structure first.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark a synchronized HashMap cache vs ConcurrentHashMap from 1 to N threads and plot where the synchronized version flatlines.

lessons.title: Escape Analysis and Scalar Replacement
concepts: Escape analysis proves an object's lifetime is method-local; scalar replacement then stores its fields in registers/stack — zero heap allocation, zero GC.
The classic beneficiaries are iterators, Optional chains, small value-like objects (Points, Money) created and consumed within one method.
Inlining is the enabler: escape analysis works best on small inlined call trees — megamorphic calls that defeat inlining also defeat scalar replacement.
Partial escape analysis (C2) handles branches where the object escapes on only some paths — the allocation is materialized lazily, only on the escaping path.

example.walkthrough: Both Points are created, read, and discarded within the method — escape analysis proves they never escape, and C2 replaces the allocations with direct field arithmetic in registers. Change the method to return a and the allocation materializes (it must live on the heap now). This is why 'avoid allocation' advice must be checked against what the JIT already does: the clean version is often already the fast version.

pitfalls: Pooling non-escaping objects — adds shared mutable state and synchronization to eliminate an allocation the JIT already removed.
Assuming all short-lived allocation is free — escape analysis has limits (size, inlining depth, escaping branches); profile before and after.
Writing 'allocation-free' code that defeats inlining — megamorphic call sites prevent the analysis that would have eliminated the allocation; clean small methods win twice.
Trusting JFR allocation counts as heap pressure — allocation events fire at the bytecode 'new'; scalar replacement happens later, in the compiler.
lessons.try_it: Write the Point example, run with -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations (debug JVM) or compare GC pressure with/without the allocation, and confirm the elimination.

lessons.title: Sealed Classes and Exhaustive Switches
concepts: Sealed classes (permits clause) close a hierarchy: only listed subtypes may extend it, so the compiler knows every possible subtype.
Exhaustive switches over sealed types (or enums) with no default are compile-checked — a new subtype without a case is a build failure, not a silent bug.
Pattern matching for switch combines type test, cast, and guard (case CardPayment c when c.isExpired()) in one readable branch.
Records pair naturally with sealed hierarchies: algebraic data types (sealed interface + record variants) model domain states the compiler can verify.

example.walkthrough: The sealed interface lists every permitted variant; the switch handles each with pattern variables — no casts, no default. When CryptoPayment is added to the permits list, this switch stops compiling until a case is added: the compiler becomes the checklist. Compare with the old instanceof ladder, where the new subtype would fall through silently and money would sit unprocessed.

pitfalls: Adding a default branch 'for safety' to an exhaustive switch — the default swallows the exhaustiveness check; the compiler can no longer warn about the missing subtype.
Sealing without updating switches — permits changes break exhaustive switches by design; that breakage is the feature, fix the switches.
Using sealed for hierarchies meant to be extended by clients — sealing is for closed domain models; framework extension points stay open (non-sealed or regular interfaces).
Pattern variables with the same name in different cases — each case has its own scope; reuse is fine, but guards (when) must come after the pattern.
lessons.try_it: Model a small domain (e.g. Shape: Circle, Rectangle, Triangle) as a sealed interface of records, write an exhaustive switch, then add a variant and observe the compile error.

lessons.title: Text Blocks, Formatting, and Unicode Done Right
concepts: Text blocks (""" """) preserve formatting verbatim — multi-line SQL, JSON, and HTML in tests become copy-pasteable and diffable.
Incidental whitespace is stripped by the compiler (the closing delimiter's indentation sets the margin); \s preserves a trailing space explicitly, \<newline> joins lines.
.formatted() on text blocks interpolates %s/%d cleanly; format-specifier mismatches fail fast instead of producing garbage strings.
Unicode escapes (\uXXXX) are processed before lexing — a \u0022 inside a comment or string can surprise; prefer explicit escapes in text blocks.

example.walkthrough: The text block holds the JSON exactly as it appears on the wire; .formatted() fills the two placeholders. The closing """ position strips the common indentation, so the value has no leading spaces. A diff on this test shows JSON changes, not escaping noise — and there are no backslashes left to get wrong.

pitfalls: Concatenating "\\"" escapes by hand — every edit risks the exact bug in the scenario; text blocks remove the hazard class.
Forgetting the closing delimiter's indentation role — misaligned """ leaves stray leading whitespace in the value; keep delimiters aligned.
Using text blocks for single-line strings — pointless; text blocks pay off at 3+ lines.
Building expected output with the same code under test — circular tests that cannot fail; hand-write expectations or use golden files from a trusted source.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite any 5+ line escaped string in a test as a text block with .formatted() and confirm the test still passes with cleaner diffs.

lessons.title: Composition Over Inheritance: The Fragile Base Class
concepts: The fragile base class problem: subclasses depend on undocumented self-call patterns of the parent; any parent change can alter subclass behavior without touching subclass code.
Composition (forwarding/delegation, often via records or explicit wrapper classes) depends on interfaces, not implementations — internal parent changes cannot re-enter your code.
Inheritance is for subtyping (is-a with substitutability, Liskov); code reuse alone is not a reason to extend — reuse is what composition and delegation are for.
When you must inherit (frameworks), document self-use: which overridable methods call which, so subclasses (including future you) know the contract.

example.walkthrough: InstrumentedSet wraps any Set and forwards calls, counting additions. If HashSet's internals change (addAll implemented differently, new internal self-calls), the wrapper is unaffected — it never overrode anything. The inheritance version (extending a concrete collection and overriding add/addAll) double-counts the moment the parent's addAll starts calling the overridden add — the exact production bug in the scenario, fixed structurally rather than by reading diffs forever.

pitfalls: Extending concrete classes for reuse — the fragile base class problem is a when, not an if, across library upgrades.
Overriding without knowing the parent's self-use contract — every override is a bet on undocumented internal call patterns.
Deep inheritance hierarchies for domain modeling — prefer flat composition of small components; hierarchies deeper than 2-3 levels are a design smell.
Using inheritance across module/library boundaries casually — inside one codebase you control both sides; across a library boundary you control neither.
lessons.try_it: Find an extends-concrete-class in a sample codebase, convert it to a delegating wrapper, and verify behavior is preserved with the existing tests.

lessons.title: Strategy Pattern with Functional Interfaces
concepts: Strategy encapsulates varying behavior behind a common interface — the selection logic (map lookup) is separate from the behaviors (implementations).
Functional interfaces (Predicate, Function, custom @FunctionalInterface) express strategies as lambdas/method refs — the pattern without the boilerplate class-per-strategy of 2004.
Open/closed in practice: new behaviors = new code + registration, never modification of existing behavior code — merges stop conflicting because files stop being shared.
Records make excellent strategy carriers when the strategy needs data (thresholds, rates) — immutable, transparent, trivially testable in isolation.

example.walkthrough: Each tier is an independent expression; the map is the only shared code, and adding ENTERPRISE is one Map.entry plus one lambda — no existing line changes. Each strategy unit-tests in isolation (no fixture for the whole ladder), and the VipPricing record shows the pattern scaling to stateful strategies. The 200-line ladder's merge conflicts disappear because there is no longer a shared file to conflict on.

pitfalls: Keeping the ladder and adding comments — comments do not fix the open/closed violation; the next tier still edits shared code.
Pushing branching logic into config files — untyped, untested, undebuggable; config is for values, not algorithms.
One giant switch instead of if-else — same shared-edit problem with nicer syntax; the pattern, not the keyword, is the fix.
Strategies that secretly depend on each other — keep strategies independent; shared preconditions belong in the selection layer, not hidden in implementations.
lessons.try_it: Extract one branch of an if-else ladder into a functional-interface strategy with a map registry; add a new variant without touching existing code.

lessons.title: Defensive Copying and True Immutability
concepts: Unmodifiable wrappers are live views of the backing collection — they prevent caller mutation but reflect owner mutation; they are access control, not immutability.
Map.copyOf/List.copyOf/Set.copyOf produce truly immutable snapshots (and reject nulls) — copy at construction, store the copy, expose the copy.
Defensive copying applies at every trust boundary: constructor inputs, getters returning collections, and deserialization — any retained alias is a future mutation.
Records help structurally: compact constructors can normalize/copy components (this.items = List.copyOf(items)), making the immutability guarantee visible in one place.

example.walkthrough: The compact constructor copies the input map before assignment, so the record never aliases the caller's mutable map, and the stored map itself is immutable. No setter, no internal mutation path, no view-vs-copy ambiguity — the type (record + immutable map) IS the guarantee, checked by construction rather than by convention. Contrast the buggy version: this.settings = Collections.unmodifiableMap(settings) retains the alias, and any later settings.put(...) is visible to all holders.

pitfalls: Wrapping with unmodifiableMap and keeping the mutable original — the view reflects later mutations; the 'immutability' is fiction.
Copying in the constructor but exposing the original field via a getter — the getter must return the copy (or another copy), never the mutable input.
Assuming records are deeply immutable — records are shallowly immutable; a record holding a mutable list is mutable through the list. Copy components.
Documenting 'do not mutate' instead of making mutation impossible — conventions are not guarantees; the type system should enforce it.
lessons.try_it: Write a class that wraps a caller-supplied map three ways (raw alias, unmodifiable view, Map.copyOf), mutate the original, and observe which holders see the change.

lessons.title: HashMap Internals: Buckets, Trees, and Capacity
concepts: HashMap indexes by (n-1) & spread(hash): spread() XORs high bits down so poor low-bit distributions still spread — but it cannot create entropy that is not there.
TREEIFY_THRESHOLD=8 converts long bins to trees; MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY=64 resizes first — the map assumes few-buckets means under-capacity, not bad hashing.
A good hashCode uses all significant fields with prime multiplication (Objects.hash or hand-rolled 31 * result + field) — constant or identity-poor hashes defeat every map optimization.
Resize doubles capacity and rehashes — O(n) amortized, but a resize storm from default 16 capacity on a 2M-entry map is itself a startup cost; size appropriately (expected/0.75).

example.walkthrough: The constant hashCode funnels every entry into a single bin regardless of capacity — 2M entries, one tree, ~21 comparisons per lookup plus cache misses. The record's default hashCode (Objects.hash over components) distributes across bins, restoring O(1) average lookups. This is also why keys must be immutable: mutating a key's hash-relevant field after insertion strands the entry in the wrong bin — the map can never find it again.

pitfalls: Constant or near-constant hashCode — defeats buckets, trees, and spreading alike; the map degrades to a slow tree/list.
Mutable keys — changing a field used by hashCode/equals after insertion orphans the entry; lookups silently return null.
Relying on treeification as a hash-quality strategy — it is a safety net for adversarial-but-varied keys, not a substitute for hashing.
Default capacity 16 for known-large maps — resize storms at startup; construct with (int)(expectedSize / 0.75f) + 1.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark HashMap get() with a constant-hashCode key vs a proper hashCode at 100k entries and observe the cliff.

lessons.title: Bounded Wildcards and Generic Methods
concepts: Generics are invariant: List<Integer> is neither List<Number> nor List<Object> — this is what prevents heap pollution (a Double in a List<Integer>).
PECS: ? extends T for producers (you read Ts out), ? super T for consumers (you put Ts in) — the mnemonic decides every wildcard.
Generic methods (<T extends Number> void add(List<T>...)) capture the type when the wildcard alone cannot express a relationship between parameters.
Type erasure means no new T[], no instanceof T at runtime — wildcards and bounds are compile-time contracts; casts through them deserve @SuppressWarnings with a comment proving safety.

example.walkthrough: The wildcard documents intent: this method writes Integers into the list but makes no promise about what reading yields (only Object is safe). ArrayList<Number> satisfies ? super Integer, so the call compiles — and the method physically cannot corrupt the list, because adding an Integer to a List<Number> is always sound. The commented-out read shows the tradeoff: consumers give up precise reads, which is exactly the PECS contract.

pitfalls: Raw types to dodge a wildcard — deletes type safety instead of expressing the constraint; -Xlint:rawtypes exists to shame this.
Unchecked casts (List<Number>)(List<?>) — compiles with a warning, fails at runtime with heap pollution; the warning was the compiler trying to help.
? extends where ? super belongs (and vice versa) — extends gives you reads but forbids writes; pick by PECS, not by what compiles first.
Wildcards in return types — forces every caller to deal with capture; use them in parameters, concrete types in returns.
lessons.try_it: Write sum(List<? extends Number>) (producer) and fill(List<? super Integer>) (consumer); try swapping the wildcards and read the compiler errors as the lesson.

lessons.title: Specialized Collections: EnumMap, EnumSet, and Primitive Maps
concepts: EnumSet: bit-vector implementation (RegularEnumSet = one long for ≤64 constants, JumboEnumSet = long[] beyond) — the most memory- and CPU-efficient set for enums, period.
EnumMap: array indexed by ordinal — O(1) without hashing, iteration in declaration order; the default map when keys are an enum.

Boxed primitives in collections (Boolean, Integer) cost 16-24 bytes per value plus GC pressure — primitive collections (Eclipse Collections, fastutil) or domain encodings (bit sets) for bulk numeric data.
Choose the collection by domain shape: fixed small universe -> bit set/enum set; enum keys -> EnumMap; identity semantics -> IdentityHashMap; insertion order -> LinkedHashMap.

example.walkthrough: Forty flags collapse into one 64-bit word; contains() compiles to a shift-and-mask — nanoseconds, zero allocation. Adding flag 41 is free (still one long); the 65th transparently switches to JumboEnumSet. Contrast the ArrayList<Boolean>: 10M references + up to 10M Boolean instances, unboxing on every check, and GC scanning all of it.

pitfalls: ArrayList<Boolean>/HashSet<Integer> for bulk flags — boxing turns bits into objects; 10-20x memory overhead plus GC pressure.
HashMap with enum keys — works, but pays hashing and entry objects; EnumMap is array-indexed and strictly better.
Ordinal-indexed arrays by hand — fragile (reordering the enum breaks data); EnumMap/EnumSet give the same performance with type safety.
Premature primitive-collection libraries for small data — EnumSet/EnumMap cover the enum cases with zero dependencies; reach for fastutil only at real numeric scale.
lessons.try_it: Measure memory (via JOL or heap dump) of ArrayList<Boolean> vs EnumSet vs BitSet for 1M flag-sets and compare.

lessons.title: Collectors: groupingBy, partitioningBy, and Downstream
concepts: groupingBy(classifier, downstream) nests arbitrarily — downstream can be counting(), summingDouble(), summarizingDouble(), mapping(), or another groupingBy.
partitioningBy(predicate) is the two-bucket special case (true/false) — clearer than groupingBy(x -> predicate.test(x)) for boolean splits.
summarizingDouble/Int/Long produce count/sum/min/max/average in one pass — the statistics object replaces hand-rolled accumulator classes.
groupingByConcurrent enables parallel collection into a ConcurrentMap — the safe parallel counterpart to the corrupted hand-rolled map.

example.walkthrough: Two levels of grouping with a statistics downstream: one pass over the sales, producing the full report tree. Each cell holds count/sum/min/max/average — the report's numbers without a single loop or mutable map in sight. Swap groupingBy for groupingByConcurrent and add .parallel() and the accumulation stays correct, because the collector (not your code) owns the merging.

pitfalls: Hand-rolled mutable accumulation with parallel streams — races and corruption; collectors own the safe merge.
Nested loops for nested grouping — O(levels) code complexity for a declarative one-liner; untestable in pieces.
collect() with a shared ArrayList supplier in parallel — the supplier must create independent containers per thread; use the built-in collectors.
Ignoring the downstream — groupingBy without a downstream gives Map<K, List<V>>; the downstream (mapping, counting, summarizing) is where the report logic lives.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a 2-level nested-loop report as composed groupingBy collectors and verify identical output on the same dataset.

lessons.title: flatMap: Streams of Streams
concepts: map: one-to-one transformation (Order -> List<LineItem>); flatMap: one-to-many (Order -> Stream<LineItem>) with concatenation — the shapes are different operations.
flatMap also flattens Optionals (opt.stream()), arrays (Arrays::stream), and nested collections uniformly — any 'container of containers' collapses the same way.
Order matters: filter BEFORE flatMap when the predicate is on the outer element (fewer streams created); filter after when it is on the inner elements.
Primitive flatMaps (flatMapToInt/Long/Double) avoid boxing when flattening numeric nests — the specialized variants exist for hot paths.

example.code:
List<LineItem> big-ticket = orders.stream()
    .flatMap(o -> o.lineItems().stream()) // Stream<LineItem>, flattened
    .filter(i -> i.price() > 100)
    .toList(); // one pass, no nesting
example.walkthrough: Each order's item list becomes a stream; flatMap concatenates them into a single Stream<LineItem>; filter and toList operate on items directly. The nested structure exists only in the domain model — the stream pipeline never sees it. Compare the nested-loop version: same result, but the loop version interleaves traversal with logic, while the stream version separates 'flatten' from 'filter'.

pitfalls: map when you need flatMap — Stream<List<X>> is the telltale; if you then loop to flatten, the operation was wrong.
flatMap with null-returning mappers — the mapper must return a stream, never null; use Stream.empty() or filter nulls first (or Objects::nonNull).
Deep flatMap chains on huge nests without considering laziness — flatMap is lazy, but each level adds per-element overhead; sometimes a loop is honestly clearer.
Forgetting that flatMap preserves encounter order for ordered streams — parallel flatMap may interleave; order matters for toList() determinism.
lessons.try_it: Take any nested collection in a sample project (orders/items, departments/employees) and rewrite the nested loop as flatMap + filter + collect.

lessons.title: Optional Done Right: map, flatMap, orElseThrow
concepts: Optional.map transforms a present value; flatMap chains Optional-returning steps without nesting — map for values, flatMap for Optionals.
Terminal operations decide the absence policy in one place: orElseThrow(() -> new DomainException(...)) for required chains, orElse/orElseGet for defaults.
Optional is for return types and chains — not for fields, not for method parameters, not for collections (empty collections already express absence).
orElse vs orElseGet: orElse evaluates its argument eagerly (wasted work / side effects even when present); orElseGet takes a Supplier and defers.

example.walkthrough: Four nullable links, zero null checks, one absence policy. If any link is empty the chain short-circuits and the terminal throws the domain exception with context. Adding a fifth nullable link is one more flatMap line — the pyramid version would add another indentation level and another chance to forget. The repository methods return Optional (findUser, not getUser-or-null), which is the API contract that makes the chain possible.

pitfalls: Optional.get() without isPresent() — the pyramid's NPE wearing a costume; orElseThrow documents the absence contract instead.
Optional as field/parameter type — serialization pain and API noise; use it for returns and chains only.
orElse with expensive/side-effecting defaults — eager evaluation runs the default even when the value is present; orElseGet defers.
Returning null from an Optional-returning method — breaks the contract the whole chain relies on; Optional.empty() is the only absent value.
lessons.try_it: Refactor one null-check pyramid into an Optional chain; verify the same inputs produce the same outputs, including the absent cases.

lessons.title: Virtual Threads: One Thread Per Task
concepts: Virtual threads are JVM-managed, cheap (KBs), and near-unlimited — thread-per-request/task becomes viable at scales where platform threads exhaust memory.
Thread.ofVirtual().start(task) and Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() are the entry points; existing ExecutorService code often migrates by changing one factory line.
Pinning: synchronized (block/method) and native calls pin the virtual thread to its carrier — prefer ReentrantLock and check JFR's VirtualThreadPinned events under load.
ThreadLocal + millions of virtual threads = memory disaster (each virtual thread carries its own map); prefer ScopedValue (Java 21+) for request-scoped context.

example.walkthrough: Each SSE connection gets its own virtual thread running plain blocking I/O code — no async rewrite, no callbacks. When handleSse blocks on the socket, the virtual thread unmounts and its carrier serves another; 10k parked virtual threads cost megabytes, not gigabytes. The try-with-resources executor (StructuredTaskScope's simpler cousin here) shuts down cleanly. Profile once under load for pinned events, replace any hot synchronized with ReentrantLock, and the architecture is done.

pitfalls: synchronized inside virtual threads at scale — pins carriers; the service 'migrates to Loom' but keeps platform-thread contention characteristics.
ThreadLocal for request context across millions of virtual threads — each virtual thread has its own ThreadLocalMap; memory explodes. Use ScopedValue.
Assuming virtual threads make blocking free — blocking still consumes the underlying resource (socket, DB connection); Loom makes WAITING cheap, not the work itself.
Pooling virtual threads — pointless; they are cheap to create. The pool was the workaround for expensive threads — remove the workaround, not the benefit.
lessons.try_it: Write a server handling 5k concurrent blocking connections with a fixed platform pool (watch it fail), then switch the executor to virtual threads and observe.

lessons.title: Structured Concurrency: Fan-Out with Deadlines
concepts: StructuredTaskScope.fork() creates child subtasks bound to the scope's lifetime — when the try-with-resources scope exits, all subtasks are complete or cancelled. No orphans.
ShutdownOnFailure: first exception cancels siblings and is thrown by join(); ShutdownOnSuccess: first result wins, rest cancelled — the two policies cover fail-fast and hedged fan-out.
Deadlines belong on the scope (joinUntil(Instant)), not on individual gets — one deadline governs the whole fan-out, and expiry cancels everything uniformly.
Subtask results compose after join(): scope.fork() returns Subtask handles; join() then subtask.get() — errors surface as structured exceptions, not ExecutionException wrapping.

example.walkthrough: Three services fan out as scoped subtasks; joinUntil enforces a single 2-second deadline for the whole operation. If the recommender hangs, the deadline expires, joinUntil throws TimeoutException, and scope exit cancels all three subtasks — no leaked threads, no orphaned connections. If users.get throws, ShutdownOnFailure cancels the siblings immediately instead of waiting for work whose result will be discarded. Compare the Future version: same happy path, but every failure mode leaks.

pitfalls: Future.get(timeout) as the 'fix' — stops waiting, abandons the task; the thread and connection leak until the slow call finishes on its own.
Submitting to a shared pool without lifecycle binding — the pool outlives the request; cancelled requests leave running tasks invisible to monitoring.
Catching exceptions per-future and continuing — partial failure handling scattered across five call sites; the scope policy centralizes it.
Nested scopes without thought — scopes compose, but each level needs its own deadline policy; a child scope without a deadline inherits the parent's hang.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a 3-way Future.get() fan-out with StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure and a deadline; inject a hanging subtask and verify cancellation.

lessons.title: ReentrantLock vs synchronized: The Pinning Problem
concepts: Pinning: synchronized blocks/methods and JNI calls prevent a virtual thread from unmounting — the carrier thread blocks instead of being reused.
ReentrantLock (java.util.concurrent.locks) unmounts properly on contention — the mechanical fix for pinned synchronized hotspots under Loom.
JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event (with stack traces) is the diagnostic: it fires exactly when pinning exceeds a threshold, naming the synchronized frame.
The rule of thumb: in virtual-thread code, default to j.u.c locks; synchronized remains fine for uncontended or platform-thread code paths.

example.walkthrough: Same mutual exclusion, different blocking behavior: under contention the ReentrantLock version parks the virtual thread (unmounted, carrier free) while the synchronized version parks the carrier. The try/finally is the non-negotiable discipline — lock without guaranteed unlock is a deadlock factory. For the cache in the scenario, this single change moves the plateau from 'carrier count' to 'actual resource limits'.

pitfalls: Leaving synchronized on contended paths after a Loom migration — the migration's headline benefit silently capped at the old thread count.
lock() without try/finally — an exception between lock and unlock wedges the lock forever; the pattern is lock-try-finally, always.
Replacing ALL synchronized reflexively — uncontended synchronized is biased-locked and nearly free; change what JFR proves is pinned and hot.
Using ReentrantLock but calling it from platform-thread pools expecting synchronized semantics — fairness and reentrancy differ subtly; match the lock to the threading model.
