lessons.try_it: Write a contended counter with synchronized vs ReentrantLock on virtual threads, capture VirtualThreadPinned events, and compare throughput at 10k threads.

lessons.title: The Module System: requires, exports, and opens
concepts: Split packages are illegal in the module system: one package, one module — the JVM fails fast where the classpath silently picked a winner.
requires declares readability (this module needs that one); exports opens a package for compile/runtime access; opens allows deep reflection (needed by frameworks like Hibernate/Jackson).
jdeps --generate-module-info analyzes JARs and drafts module-info.java — the migration starting point for any modularization effort.
The unnamed module (classpath) reads everything but exports nothing formally — mixing classpath and module path is the pragmatic migration corridor.

example.walkthrough: requires names real dependencies (no more ClassNotFound roulette); exports defines the public surface (everything else is encapsulated even from reflection); opens grants Jackson reflective access to DTOs without exporting them to everyone. Strong encapsulation is the payoff: internal packages are unreachable even via setAccessible, which is why libraries modularize — their internals stop being accidental public API.

pitfalls: Staying on the classpath to dodge split packages — the nondeterminism remains; the module system just stopped letting you ignore it.
exports for everything 'to be safe' — defeats encapsulation; export the API, open narrowly for frameworks.
opens vs exports confusion — exports is compile+runtime access; opens is runtime reflection; frameworks need opens, clients need exports.
Automatic modules as a permanent state — they are a migration bridge; unnamed-package JARs still cannot express or enforce boundaries.
lessons.try_it: Create two JARs with a split package, observe the module-path failure, then shade-relocate one and watch it resolve.

lessons.title: NIO.2: Paths, Files, and WatchService
concepts: WatchService delivers change notifications, not a complete ledger — coalescing and OVERFLOW mean events are hints; the directory scan is the truth.
The robust pattern: on any event (especially OVERFLOW), list the directory and reconcile with processed state (a Set<Path> or database of handled files).
Register the directory (not files) with ENTRY_CREATE/ENTRY_MODIFY/ENTRY_DELETE; take the WatchKey, pollEvents(), and always key.reset() — a key that is not reset stops delivering.
For recursive trees, register each subdirectory and handle ENTRY_CREATE of new directories by registering them too — WatchService is not recursive by itself.

example.walkthrough: Every event — create, modify, or overflow — triggers rescan(dir), which lists the directory and processes anything not in the handled set. Coalesced events cannot cause skips (the scan finds the file), OVERFLOW cannot cause skips (the scan is unconditional), and key.reset() keeps delivery alive. The event kinds still matter for efficiency (a modify-only event can skip full reprocessing), but correctness never depends on receiving every event.

pitfalls: Processing only received events — the silent-skip bug; OVERFLOW exists precisely because events get dropped.
Forgetting key.reset() — the key becomes invalid and the watcher silently stops; always reset in a finally-ish flow.
Assuming recursive watching — only registered directories are watched; new subdirectories need explicit registration on ENTRY_CREATE.
Blocking forever on watcher.take() without shutdown handling — the importer cannot stop cleanly; use poll with timeout and a poison-pill or interrupt discipline.
lessons.try_it: Write a WatchService importer, flood the directory with 10k files at once, and verify zero skips via the rescan pattern (then break it by removing rescan to see the skips).

lessons.title: Serialization Safety: serialVersionUID and Records
concepts: An explicit serialVersionUID makes the serialized form a deliberate contract: same UID + compatible change = successful deserialization with defaults for new fields.
Compatible vs incompatible evolution: adding fields/methods is compatible; changing field types, class hierarchy, or removing fields breaks it — bump the UID intentionally.
Java native deserialization of untrusted bytes is a critical vulnerability class (gadget chains) — validate with ObjectInputFilter or avoid it entirely for network input.
Records are serialization-friendly (canonical constructor restores invariants); for new systems prefer JSON/Jackson or protobuf — versioned, language-neutral, inspectable.

example.walkthrough: With serialVersionUID = 1L declared, the 2.4 reader accepts 2.3 bytes: lastSeen arrives null (documented default), no exception. The UID bump becomes a conscious decision for incompatible changes, not an accident of adding a field. The filter line is the security half: even for trusted caches, a serial filter bounds what classes may materialize — defense in depth against gadget chains.

pitfalls: Omitting serialVersionUID — every structural change becomes an accidental format break; the compiler warning exists for this reason.
Deserializing untrusted bytes with native serialization — the gadget-chain attack class; use filters or (better) a data format.
Changing field types and keeping the UID — silent data corruption is worse than InvalidClassException; bump the UID on incompatible changes.
toString()/parsing as a serialization strategy — no versioning, no escaping discipline, breaks on the first special character; use a real format.
lessons.try_it: Serialize an object, add a field, and observe the failure without an explicit UID — then declare one and watch compatible evolution work.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The bootcamp has four content types with different jobs: lessons build mental models, scenarios build decision-making under pressure, labs build hands-on fluency, mocks build exam stamina.
The diagnostic loop: drill scenarios -> identify weak domains -> study those lessons -> hands-on try-it -> re-drill -> mock. Repeat until the weak list is empty.
Time-box study in focused 50-minute blocks per domain; context-switching across six domains in one session destroys retention.
Track your scenario accuracy per domain over time — a rising trend in your weakest domain is the signal the loop is working; flat scores mean the study method (not the effort) needs changing.

example.code:
Week 1: diagnostic scenario pass (all domains, untimed, honest answers).
Week 2-3: lessons + try-it for the two weakest domains; re-drill those domains.
Week 4: labs for weak domains; full mock under timed conditions.
Repeat: the weakest domain from the mock becomes next week's focus.
example.walkthrough: This four-week loop turns the content pile into a training program: diagnosis directs effort, lessons and labs build the missing capability, and the mock measures transfer under pressure. Adjust the timeline to your deadline, but keep the loop order — diagnosis before study, study before re-test, always.

pitfalls: Reading linearly cover-to-cover — equal time on strong and weak areas; the diagnostic exists to prevent exactly this.
Taking the mock before any study and treating the score as a verdict — the first mock is a diagnostic, not a judgment; its job is to aim your effort.
Skipping the try-it exercises — reading about virtual threads is not the same as starting 5k of them; fluency needs the keyboard.
Cramming all domains in one marathon session — interleaving is good, exhaustion is not; spaced, focused blocks beat heroic sessions.
lessons.try_it: Run one full diagnostic scenario pass this week and write down your three weakest domains — that list is your study plan.

lessons.title: Study Strategy for Java Mastery
concepts: Active recall over re-reading: close the lesson and reconstruct the concept (the code, the pitfall, the why) from memory — the struggle is the learning.
The Feynman technique: explain each concept in plain words as if teaching it; the exact sentence where you stumble names your gap.
Spaced repetition for facts (GC flags, collection complexities), interleaved practice for skills (alternate domains per session once basics are solid).
Prediction before execution: for every code example, guess the output first — wrong guesses are the most memorable lessons.

example.code: For each lesson: (1) read the concepts, (2) close the page and write the example from memory, (3) predict-then-run the try-it, (4) explain the pitfalls aloud in your own words, (5) drill the domain's scenarios tomorrow (spaced), not today.
example.walkthrough: This five-step protocol converts each lesson from 'content consumed' to 'skill built': reconstruction tests recall, prediction creates feedback, explanation tests understanding, and next-day drilling tests retention. It is slower per lesson than reading — and several times faster per retained skill, which is the only metric that matters.

pitfalls: Re-reading lessons and calling it study — fluency illusion; recognition feels like knowledge until you must produce.
Passive video at 2x with no practice — exposure without retrieval decays within days.
Studying only past questions — interviews twist; concepts transfer, question-memorization does not.
Marathon cramming the night before — sleep consolidates memory; the all-nighter trades retention for exhaustion.
lessons.try_it: Pick one lesson, apply the five-step protocol, and notice where step 2 (write from memory) exposes gaps that reading hid.

lessons.title: Course Map: The Java Landscape
concepts: Layer 1 — Language: language-core, oop-design, collections-generics, streams-lambdas. The vocabulary: what the code says.
Layer 2 — Execution: jvm-internals, concurrency-virtual-threads, modules-jars-io. The machinery: how the code runs.
Layer 3 — Ecosystem: build-tools, testing-junit, spring-boot. The profession: how the code ships.
Layer 4 — Mastery: jvm-performance. The optimization: how the code runs FASTER — only meaningful atop layers 1-3.

example.code:
Prerequisite chain: language-core -> collections -> streams -> concurrency -> jvm-internals -> jvm-performance.
Parallel track: build-tools + testing-junit alongside layer 1; spring-boot after testing.
Capstone last: it integrates all four layers into one shipped service.
example.walkthrough: The chain shows the one true ordering constraint; the parallel track shows what can interleave. If a layer-3 lesson confuses you, the map tells you exactly which layer-1 or layer-2 lesson to revisit — confusion becomes a pointer, not a feeling. The capstone sits at the end deliberately: it is the integration test of the whole map.

pitfalls: Treating all domains as independent — the confusion in jvm-performance is usually a missing prerequisite, and the map names it.
Studying spring-boot before testing-junit — you will write untestable services and call it Spring's fault.
Doing the capstone first 'to see the big picture' — the big picture without the layers is just overwhelm.
Ignoring modules-jars-io as 'ops stuff' — classpath/module failures are the most common 'works on my machine' class in Java.
lessons.try_it: Draw the four layers from memory, place each domain, and mark your current position — then study the next layer down from any confusion.

lessons.title: Assessment Strategy: Java Interviews and Exams
concepts: Live coding: practice thinking aloud while coding — interviewers score the reasoning trace, not just the green tests; narrate tradeoffs as you type.
Concept grilling: for each lesson, be able to answer 'why does this exist?' and 'when would you NOT use it?' — depth questions probe the boundaries.
System design: structure answers as requirements -> constraints -> options -> decision -> tradeoffs; the capstone build is your rehearsal artifact.
Exams: read every option before choosing — exam distractors are engineered from common misconceptions (this bootcamp's scenarios train exactly this discrimination).

example.code:
Two weeks before: daily 45-min live-coding reps (think aloud, record yourself).
One week before: concept blitz — explain 10 random lesson titles aloud, 2 minutes each.
Three days before: full mock under timed conditions; review every wrong scenario's 'why'.
Day before: light review + sleep. Cramming the night before degrades recall.
example.walkthrough: The taper mirrors athletic training: skill reps while fresh, concept consolidation, then a full dress rehearsal (the mock) with review, then rest. Recording yourself on coding reps feels awkward and works — you hear the moments your narration goes silent, which are the moments an interviewer starts doubting. The mock is the only honest predictor; everything else is practice.

pitfalls: Silent coding in interviews — the interviewer cannot score thinking they cannot hear; narrate continuously.
Reciting definitions for concept questions — 'volatile ensures visibility' without the cache-coherence story fails the follow-up; know the why.
Answering system design with a single solution — interviews score tradeoff reasoning; present options, decide, justify.
Night-before cramming — sleep consolidates procedural memory; the cram session costs more recall than it buys.
lessons.try_it: Record yourself explaining one lesson's 'why' in 2 minutes; listen for the sentence where you hedge — that is your next study target.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture: The Order Processing Service
concepts: Layered architecture: controller (HTTP contract, validation) -> service (transactions, domain rules) -> repository (persistence) — each layer has one job and one test strategy.
Transactional outbox: domain event rows written in the same transaction as the business data; a relay publishes them — exactly-once effects without distributed transactions.
Virtual threads for request concurrency: blocking code at 5k concurrent requests without the reactive learning curve.
Operability as a feature: health groups, Micrometer metrics, structured logging, and trace IDs from day one — the team that inherits it needs signals, not archaeology.

example.code:
Module layout: com.shop.order (controller/service/repo), com.shop.payment (client + outbox), com.shop.notify (relay), com.shop.admin (reporting queries).
Data: orders + outbox tables in Postgres (Testcontainers in tests).
Runtime: Spring Boot 3, Java 21, virtual threads, Actuator/Prometheus.
Acceptance: kill -9 mid-order -> restart -> order and notification both present exactly once.
example.walkthrough: The layout makes the architecture reviewable: each package owns a bounded context, the outbox table is the reliability mechanism made visible, and the acceptance test (kill -9 mid-request) is the requirement 'survive restarts' turned into an executable specification. Virtual threads and Actuator are not garnish — they are the answers to the stated concurrency and operability requirements, chosen in the architecture phase rather than bolted on later.

pitfalls: Microservices for a 5k-user service — distributed transactions, deployment topology, and observability costs for scale you do not have; modular monolith first.
Dual-writes (DB then queue, or queue then DB) — crash between the two loses or duplicates; the outbox exists because dual-writes are broken.
No acceptance test for the reliability requirement — 'survives restarts' without a kill -9 test is a wish, not an architecture.
Skipping operability ('we will add metrics later') — later never comes; unobservable services are undebuggable services.
lessons.try_it: Draw the module diagram and the outbox flow for the order service; write the kill -9 acceptance test FIRST (it defines done).

lessons.title: Capstone Build Guide: From Zero to Running
concepts: Build vertical slices, not horizontal layers: each slice (persist -> serve -> notify) is end-to-end testable and demoable on its own.
Test each layer with its cheapest effective strategy: Testcontainers for repositories, constructor-injected unit tests for services, @WebMvcTest for controllers.
The outbox relay gets its own slice with the kill -9 acceptance test — reliability is a feature with a test, not a hope.
Load-test with virtual threads BEFORE declaring done: 5k concurrent is a requirement, and requirements get tests (a JMH/Gatling-style run, not 'it felt fast').

example.code:
./mvnw verify                    # slices 1-3: unit + slice + integration tests
./mvnw -Dtest=OutboxIT verify      # slice 4: kill -9 resilience test
./mvnw -Dtest=LoadIT verify        # slice 5: 5k concurrent virtual-thread run
curl localhost:8080/actuator/health # slice 6: operability signals live
example.walkthrough: Each command is a slice's definition of done: the standard verify runs the fast pyramid, the outbox test proves crash safety, the load test proves the concurrency requirement, and the health endpoint proves operability. A slice is not done when the code is written — it is done when its command is green. This is what 'every step verifiable' means in practice.

pitfalls: Big-bang integration at the end — all wiring errors discovered simultaneously, when they are hardest to attribute.
Testing only through the full stack — slow, flaky, and diagnostically useless; slice tests isolate layers.
Skipping the kill -9 test ('we trust the outbox') — the outbox is a mechanism; the test is the proof.
Declaring the load requirement met without a load test — 'should handle 5k' is not engineering; measured 5k is.
lessons.try_it: Implement slice 1 (domain + Testcontainers persistence) and get ./mvnw verify green before writing any controller code.

lessons.title: Capstone Packaging: Demo and Writeup
concepts: Reproducible packaging: wrapper + locked deps + layered image/compose — 'clone and run' works on a stranger's machine, which is the demo bar.
Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): one short record per major choice (outbox vs dual-write, virtual threads vs reactive) with context, decision, consequences — the interview prep writes itself.
The demo script: a fixed 5-minute narrative (happy path -> failure injection -> recovery proof) — rehearsed, timed, and resilient to questions.
The writeup: problem, constraints, architecture, key tradeoffs, what you would do with 10x scale — this document is the take-home interview artifact.

example.code:
git clone <repo> && cd order-service
./mvnw -o clean verify      # reproducible, offline-capable build
docker compose up --build     # Postgres + app, one command
./demo.sh                     # 5-min scripted demo incl. kill -9 recovery
example.walkthrough: Three commands from clone to demo: the build proves reproducibility, compose proves runnable packaging, demo.sh proves the reliability story. An interviewer (or hiring manager) can run this without your help — that independence is the difference between 'a project' and 'a shipped artifact'. The ADRs in docs/adr/ answer 'why' before it is asked.

pitfalls: No wrapper/lockfile — the demo fails on the interviewer's machine; the project is un-runnable by strangers.
No ADR/decision log — 'why outbox?' gets a rambling answer instead of a crisp record; judgment is invisible.
Demoing only the happy path — anyone can demo success; the kill -9 recovery is what makes the demo memorable.
Deploying the capstone to real production for the demo — unnecessary risk and cost; compose locally, demo locally.
lessons.try_it: Write the README's 'How to run' section and the first ADR (outbox decision); time a full clone-to-demo run.

simulations.title: The vanishing element
simulations.brief: A cleanup loop removes expired sessions from a list — and crashes with ConcurrentModificationException on the second run.

steps.symptom: First run fine, second run throws ConcurrentModificationException inside the loop.
options: Read line 31: the enhanced for-loop holds an iterator, and removing directly from the list invalidates it
The list is too large; increase the heap
Sessions expire too fast; lengthen the timeout
The exception is random; rerun until it passes
steps.explain: The enhanced for loop uses an iterator under the hood; structural modification outside iterator.remove() trips the fail-fast check — intermittently, depending on timing.

options: Remove via the iterator (iterator.remove()) or collect-then-remove after the loop
steps.explain: Either remove through the iterator you are iterating with, or gather the expired sessions and remove them after the loop — both keep the iterator's view consistent.

steps.symptom: Fix applied with iterator.remove(). Verify correctness.
options: Confirm no expired session survives and no live session is removed — run the session-count assertion
Confirm the list is now empty
steps.explain: Compile-success is not correctness: assert the postcondition — every expired session gone, every live session kept.

simulations.debrief: Fail-fast iterators punish structural modification during traversal. Remove through the iterator — or after the loop — and verify the postcondition, not just the compile.

simulations.title: Checked or unchecked?
simulations.brief: A method can fail two ways: a missing config file, and a null item in a list. Decide how each failure should be modeled.

steps.text: readConfig() may not find config.yaml on disk. How should this failure surface?

choices.label: Checked exception (e.g. IOException): the caller must handle or declare it — a missing file is recoverable and expected
choices.feedback: Right: recoverable, external, expected — the textbook case for a checked exception.

choices.label: Unchecked exception: let it crash
choices.feedback: A missing config file is foreseeable — crashing without a declared contract hides a recoverable situation.

choices.label: Return null and document nothing
choices.feedback: Null returns push the failure downstream as a NullPointerException. Declare it instead.

steps.text: process(items) receives a list that must never contain null — a null means the caller broke the contract. How should this surface?

choices.label: Unchecked exception (IllegalArgumentException): a programming error, not a recoverable condition
choices.feedback: Right: contract violations are bugs — fail fast and loudly with an unchecked exception.

choices.label: Checked exception: force every caller to catch it
choices.feedback: Checked exceptions for programming errors just produce empty catch blocks.

choices.label: Silently skip null items
choices.feedback: Silent skipping hides the caller's bug and corrupts downstream results.

simulations.debrief: Checked exceptions model recoverable, expected failures (missing file); unchecked exceptions model programming errors (null where forbidden). Match the mechanism to the failure's nature.

sections.heading: Language Core
items: String literals — are interned (one shared instance per distinct literal), so == can appear to work in tests, but a runtime-built string is a different object with equal content. equals() compares content — always use it for value comparison.
Integer division — promoting one operand to double before dividing (done * 100.0 / total) performs floating-point division; cast back to int for display.
Switch expressions — a switch expression is an expression: it produces a value, so no mutable accumulator is needed.
Common trap — var works anywhere a type appears.
Common trap — arrow syntax only works for enums.
Common trap — switch expressions cannot have a default.
Common trap — records are syntax sugar for HashMap.

sections.heading: OOP & Design
items: Overriding — Overriding equals without hashCode leaves the default identity hash, so logically-equal keys scatter across buckets and lookups miss.

Default — Default methods narrowed the gap, but state, constructors, and single-inheritance still distinguish them. A default method provides an implementation inside the interface, so adding one does not break existing implementers — they inherit it.
Interface evolution — apply it to every intended override, including interface implementations.
Immutability — true immutability requires copying mutable inputs at construction and returning copies (or immutable views) from getters.
Common trap — use abstract classes whenever data is involved.
Common trap — there is no difference since Java 8 default methods.
Common trap — sealed classes cannot be implemented at all.
Common trap — mark the new method abstract and ship a migration guide.

sections.heading: Collections & Generics
items: Type erasure — generics are erased at compile time: at runtime a Cache<String> is just Cache, so the JVM could not enforce new T[]'s type safety (arrays are covariant and reified, generics are invariant and erased — the combination is unsound).
PECS — producer-extends (read from it), consumer-super (write to it — List<? super Integer> accepts Integer adds).
Producer extends — ? extends Number means 'a List of some specific subtype of Number, we know not which' — it could be List<Double>, where an Integer does not belong.
Common trap — arrays of generics are allowed since Java 10.
Common trap — the compiler cannot verify autoboxing through wildcards.
